st.rcm.chitrakoot_sabha.title: The family council at Chitrakoot
st.rcm.chitrakoot_sabha.lesson: In family conflict, let each speak; name love plainly; lift needless shame.
st.rcm.chitrakoot_sabha.summary: Vasishtha asks how Ram can be brought home, noting that grieving people cannot judge well. Bharat recalls a brother who never broke his heart and let him win at games, and blames himself. Ram tells him his shame is needless, that love and hostility cannot be hidden, and asks him to say freely what he wants.

st.rcm.kaushalya_and_sunayana.title: Janaka's family joins the council
st.rcm.kaushalya_and_sunayana.lesson: When you are too close to a decision, say so, and speak briefly and honestly.
st.rcm.kaushalya_and_sunayana.summary: Sita's parents arrive and the two families grieve together. Kausalya tells Sunayana that people, like gold, are proved by time. Janaka asks Bharat to decide, and Bharat declines: duty and self-interest pull apart, hatred is blind and love cannot reason, so he will follow Ram's wish. His few words leave the whole court in awe.

st.rcm.sita_with_her_parents.title: Sita meets her parents in her ascetic's dress
st.rcm.sita_with_her_parents.lesson: A parent's respect for a child's chosen hardship is a greater gift than rescue.
st.rcm.sita_with_her_parents.summary: Her parents see their daughter for the first time since the wedding: bark cloth, no ornaments, living in a hut. The women of Mithila break down at the sight. She is brought to her parents' tent for the evening.

st.rcm.bharat_and_the_sandals.title: Bharat rules from a hut for fourteen years
st.rcm.bharat_and_the_sandals.lesson: You can live amid plenty without being owned by it.
st.rcm.bharat_and_the_sandals.summary: Bharat places Ram's sandals on the throne and lives outside the city in a hut, sleeping on grass, fasting, governing only as a caretaker. The palace's riches are all around him and do not touch him, like a bee in a champak garden.

st.rcm.jayant_no_shelter.title: Jayant the crow: shelter for the offender
st.rcm.jayant_no_shelter.lesson: Consequences may remain, but the one who turns back is still taken in.
st.rcm.jayant_no_shelter.summary: Indra's son, disguised as a crow, pecks Sita's foot to test Ram's power. Ram's straw arrow chases him through every world; no god will shelter him. Narada sends him back to Ram, where he falls at his feet admitting he reaped what he sowed. Ram lets him go with the loss of one eye.

st.rcm.sutikshna_too_unworthy_to_hope.title: Sutikshna runs to meet Ram
st.rcm.sutikshna_too_unworthy_to_hope.lesson: You don't have to feel qualified; the one with nowhere else to go is the one he loves.
st.rcm.sutikshna_too_unworthy_to_hope.summary: A young sage hears Ram is near and runs out, sure he has no devotion, wisdom or discipline worth anything, trusting only that Ram loves those with nowhere else to go. Lost in love he wanders, dances, forgets the way; Ram watches from behind a tree, then lifts him up and holds him. Asked for a boon, the sage says only: may this one pride never leave me, that I am his.

st.rcm.maricha_two_deaths.title: Maricha caught between two deaths
st.rcm.maricha_two_deaths.lesson: A boss who threatens you into wrongdoing leaves no good option; see it early.
st.rcm.maricha_two_deaths.summary: Ravana orders his uncle Maricha to become a golden deer to lure Ram away. Maricha warns him that Ram cannot be defeated, but Ravana threatens him. Seeing death either way, Maricha reasons that it never pays to cross a powerful master, and chooses death at Ram's hands over death at Ravana's.

st.rcm.ram_asks_the_trees.title: Jatayu's last fight and Ram's grief
st.rcm.ram_asks_the_trees.lesson: Standing up for someone matters, even when you cannot win.
st.rcm.ram_asks_the_trees.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut and searches the forest, asking birds and trees if they have seen Sita. He finds the old vulture Jatayu dying; he had fought Ravana alone to stop the abduction. Ram tells him that for one whose heart is set on others' good, nothing is out of reach, and performs his funeral rites himself, as a son would.

st.rcm.jatayu_old_and_outmatched.title: Jatayu dies in Ram's lap
st.rcm.jatayu_old_and_outmatched.lesson: Nothing you do for love is small; it is honoured like family.
st.rcm.jatayu_old_and_outmatched.summary: Searching for Sita, Ram finds the old vulture who fought Ravana to save her, dying. Ram touches his head and the bird's pain leaves. Jatayu refuses Ram's offer to heal him: the one whose name people pray to say at death is in front of his eyes. He asks only for devotion, and Ram, in tears, performs his last rites with his own hands.

st.rcm.shabari_waited_and_was_taught.title: Ram visits Shabari
st.rcm.shabari_waited_and_was_taught.lesson: What counts is the heart you bring, not who you are on paper.
st.rcm.shabari_waited_and_was_taught.summary: An old forest woman, Shabari, has waited years for Ram. When he comes she washes his feet and feeds him roots and fruit, and he praises every bite. He tells her he recognises only the bond of devotion and describes nine forms of it, ending with contentment, not hunting faults, and being simple and without guile.

st.rcm.hanuman_forgot_his_master.title: Hanuman meets Ram
st.rcm.hanuman_forgot_his_master.lesson: You don't need the right method; being his is enough, and he weeps to have you back.
st.rcm.hanuman_forgot_his_master.summary: Sent by a frightened Sugriva, Hanuman goes disguised as a brahmin to question two strangers. When Ram names himself, Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet speechless, then gently complains that Ram forgot him. He says he knows no method of worship and relies on Ram as a child relies on its mother. Ram lifts him up, holds him, cools him with his own tears, and tells him he is twice as dear as Lakshman.

st.rcm.sugriva_what_a_friend_is.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
st.rcm.sugriva_what_a_friend_is.lesson: A friend treats your trouble as bigger than their own.
st.rcm.sugriva_what_a_friend_is.summary: Hanuman, sent to check whether the two strangers are Bali's spies, recognises Ram and brings him to Sugriva, who has been driven out by his brother. Before a fire as witness they become friends, and Ram describes what friendship asks: your friend's small trouble is a mountain, your own is dust; steer him right, hide his faults, love him more in hard times.

st.rcm.ram_waits_out_the_rains.title: Ram's monsoon and autumn lessons
st.rcm.ram_waits_out_the_rains.lesson: Nature keeps teaching: steadiness, humility, patience, and saving for the dry season.
st.rcm.ram_waits_out_the_rains.summary: Waiting out the rains on a mountain, Ram points out lessons to Lakshman in each sight: clouds bow low when full, mountains take the rain as the steady take harsh words, small streams swagger, ponds fill drop by drop, autumn sun dries the puddles as contentment dries greed, and fish panic as the water shrinks.

st.rcm.sugriva_forgets_his_friend.title: Sugriva forgets his promise
st.rcm.sugriva_forgets_his_friend.lesson: Success and comfort make us forget who helped us; admit it quickly and make it right.
st.rcm.sugriva_forgets_his_friend.summary: The rains end and Sugriva, now king, has forgotten his promise to search for Sita. Ram is hurt; Lakshman storms into the city in anger. Hanuman had already nudged Sugriva, who comes out, admits that comfort intoxicated him, and sends search parties in every direction.

st.rcm.search_party_past_deadline.title: Sampati's burned wings
st.rcm.search_party_past_deadline.lesson: Even after the fall your pride caused, you can still be useful, and hope can return.
st.rcm.search_party_past_deadline.summary: The search party, past its deadline with no news, sits down by the sea to die. A huge old vulture, Sampati, overhears them talking of his brother Jatayu. He tells them how pride once made him fly too close to the sun and burn his wings; a sage told him they would grow back when he helped Ram's messengers. He tells them where Sita is, and his wings grow back as he speaks.

st.rcm.sampati_wings_regrow.title: Sampati's burned wings
st.rcm.sampati_wings_regrow.lesson: Even after the fall your pride caused, you can still be useful, and hope can return.
st.rcm.sampati_wings_regrow.summary: The search party, past its deadline with no news, sits down by the sea to die. A huge old vulture, Sampati, overhears them talking of his brother Jatayu. He tells them how pride once made him fly too close to the sun and burn his wings; a sage told him they would grow back when he helped Ram's messengers. He tells them where Sita is, and his wings grow back as he speaks.

st.rcm.jambavan_why_so_silent.title: Jambavant reminds Hanuman of his strength
st.rcm.jambavan_why_so_silent.lesson: Sometimes we need someone else to remind us what we can do; and the old can be that someone.
st.rcm.jambavan_why_so_silent.summary: Nobody can leap the ocean. Old Jambavant admits honestly that he is no longer young. Then he turns to the silent Hanuman and asks why he sits quiet: what task in the world is too hard for him? Hanuman grows to the size of a mountain.

st.rcm.hanuman_no_rest_and_surasa.title: Hanuman meets Surasa on the way
st.rcm.hanuman_no_rest_and_surasa.lesson: Meet obstacles with flexibility: sometimes bigger, sometimes smaller, never stuck.
st.rcm.hanuman_no_rest_and_surasa.summary: Leaping the ocean, Hanuman refuses to rest on a friendly mountain until the work is done. Surasa blocks him and opens her jaws; he doubles his size each time she widens them, then shrinks tiny and slips in and out. A demon that catches flyers by grabbing their shadows tries the same trick, and he sees through it at once.

st.rcm.lankini_struck_awake.title: Lankini at the gate of Lanka
st.rcm.lankini_struck_awake.lesson: Carry what you love into the hard place, and the hard place changes.
st.rcm.lankini_struck_awake.summary: Entering Lanka at night as small as a mosquito, Hanuman is caught by Lankini, the city's guardian. One blow of his fist floors her; she remembers a prophecy that this means the city's end, and blesses him: a moment of good company outweighs heaven, and if he carries Ram in his heart, poison will turn to nectar.

st.rcm.vibhishan_tongue_among_teeth.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
st.rcm.vibhishan_tongue_among_teeth.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.
st.rcm.vibhishan_tongue_among_teeth.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.

st.rcm.sita_asks_for_a_pyre.title: Hanuman reaches Sita
st.rcm.sita_asks_for_a_pyre.lesson: When someone is near despair, a message that they are remembered can carry them.
st.rcm.sita_asks_for_a_pyre.summary: Sita, captive and threatened by Ravana, has nearly lost hope; only the guard Trijata has been kind. Hanuman drops Ram's ring from a tree, then tells her Ram's whole story. Sita says he has been her ship in a sea of separation; he gives her Ram's message that speaking of pain helps, but there is no one to tell, and asks her to wait a few days more.

st.rcm.trijata_the_one_kind_guard.title: Hanuman reaches Sita
st.rcm.trijata_the_one_kind_guard.lesson: When someone is near despair, a message that they are remembered can carry them.
st.rcm.trijata_the_one_kind_guard.summary: Sita, captive and threatened by Ravana, has nearly lost hope; only the guard Trijata has been kind. Hanuman drops Ram's ring from a tree, then tells her Ram's whole story. Sita says he has been her ship in a sea of separation; he gives her Ram's message that speaking of pain helps, but there is no one to tell, and asks her to wait a few days more.

st.rcm.ram_message_no_one_to_tell.title: Hanuman reaches Sita
st.rcm.ram_message_no_one_to_tell.lesson: When someone is near despair, a message that they are remembered can carry them.
st.rcm.ram_message_no_one_to_tell.summary: Sita, captive and threatened by Ravana, has nearly lost hope; only the guard Trijata has been kind. Hanuman drops Ram's ring from a tree, then tells her Ram's whole story. Sita says he has been her ship in a sea of separation; he gives her Ram's message that speaking of pain helps, but there is no one to tell, and asks her to wait a few days more.

st.rcm.hanuman_bound_before_ravana.title: Hanuman speaks plainly to Ravana
st.rcm.hanuman_bound_before_ravana.lesson: Speak truth to power calmly, and afterwards don't take the credit.
st.rcm.hanuman_bound_before_ravana.summary: Bound and dragged before Ravana, Hanuman feels no shame and tells the most powerful man in the world, calmly, to return Sita: wealth with no deep source dries up like a rain-fed river. Ravana orders his tail set on fire; Hanuman burns Lanka and returns. Back before Ram, he insists none of it was his own greatness.

st.rcm.hanuman_gives_the_credit_away.title: Ram cannot repay Hanuman
st.rcm.hanuman_gives_the_credit_away.lesson: Do the work, give away the credit, and ask only to keep loving.
st.rcm.hanuman_gives_the_credit_away.summary: Back from Lanka, Hanuman tells Ram how Sita survives: his name guards her day and night. Ram, in tears, asks whether one who relies on him can meet calamity; Hanuman answers that the only calamity is forgetting him. Ram says he can never repay Hanuman and cannot even look him in the face; Hanuman falls at his feet and will not get up. Offered anything, he asks only for unwavering devotion, and credits every deed to Ram.

st.rcm.mandodari_warning_dismissed.title: Mandodari pleads, the ministers flatter
st.rcm.mandodari_warning_dismissed.lesson: Beware a circle that only tells you what you want to hear.
st.rcm.mandodari_warning_dismissed.summary: Mandodari takes Ravana aside and begs him to return Sita before it is too late. He laughs at her fear and goes to court, where his ministers tell him only what pleases him. Tulsidas notes that when advisers, doctors and teachers speak only to please, ruin comes quickly.

st.rcm.vibhishan_kicked_for_counsel.title: Vibhishan speaks up and is kicked
st.rcm.vibhishan_kicked_for_counsel.lesson: Say the hard thing with respect; if you are struck for it, you may go.
st.rcm.vibhishan_kicked_for_counsel.summary: Vibhishan, bowing to his brother, advises him to return Sita: good sense and bad sense live in every heart, and Ravana is feeding the wrong one. Ravana kicks him. Vibhishan still says Ravana is like a father to him, and then he leaves, telling him not to blame him.

st.rcm.vibhishan_refuge_debate.title: Vibhishan crosses over
st.rcm.vibhishan_refuge_debate.lesson: Leaving a bad place takes courage; a good leader receives people without suspicion first.
st.rcm.vibhishan_refuge_debate.summary: Vibhishan crosses the sea to Ram. Sugriva suspects a spy; Ram says he never turns away anyone who comes for refuge, and that only a clean heart, without deceit, reaches him. He embraces Vibhishan, asks how he kept his goodness among the wicked, and crowns him king of Lanka before the war has even begun.

st.rcm.ram_and_the_ocean.title: Three days at the ocean: humble first, firm after
st.rcm.ram_and_the_ocean.lesson: Always ask humbly first. But don't let humility be taken for weakness.
st.rcm.ram_and_the_ocean.summary: On Vibhishan's advice, Ram first asks the ocean politely to let his army cross, and waits three days. When nothing changes, he takes up his bow, observing that counsel to the unwilling is like seed on barren soil. The ocean appears, apologises, and shows him how to build a bridge.

st.rcm.angad_the_envoy.title: Angad in Ravana's court
st.rcm.angad_the_envoy.lesson: Under insult, keep your purpose; a steady mind does not leave what is right.
st.rcm.angad_the_envoy.summary: Ram sends Angad as envoy, asking him to speak so the work gets done and it does Ravana good too. In court Ravana insults Angad, his dead father and his lord. Angad bears it, remembering that a lion gains no glory by killing a jackal. At last he plants his foot and dares anyone to move it; no warrior can.

st.rcm.ram_lament_for_lakshman.title: Lakshman falls; Hanuman brings the mountain
st.rcm.ram_lament_for_lakshman.lesson: When someone you love is ill, urgency and hope go together.
st.rcm.ram_lament_for_lakshman.summary: Lakshman is struck down by Meghnad's spear. The physician Sushena names a herb on a far mountain, and Hanuman races there, sees through a demon disguised as a sage, and, not recognising the herb, carries the whole peak. Over Ayodhya Bharat shoots him down by mistake, then revives him and helps him on. At midnight Ram holds Lakshman and grieves aloud for a brother who left everything for him; Hanuman arrives just in time.

st.rcm.kumbhakarna_tells_his_brother.title: Kumbhakarna fights for a brother he knows is wrong
st.rcm.kumbhakarna_tells_his_brother.lesson: Siblings can choose differently and still bless each other.
st.rcm.kumbhakarna_tells_his_brother.summary: Woken to fight, Kumbhakarna tells Ravana plainly he was wrong to take Sita and should have consulted him first. Still he goes out to fight for his brother. On the field he meets Vibhishan, who chose Ram, and instead of cursing him, he blesses him as the pride of their family.

st.rcm.dharma_rath.title: The chariot that wins
st.rcm.dharma_rath.lesson: Inner qualities are the real equipment for a hard fight.
st.rcm.dharma_rath.summary: Ravana rides out in a chariot; Ram stands on foot, and Vibhishan worries. Ram describes the chariot that really wins: courage and patience as its wheels, truth and character as its flag, strength, judgement, self-control and kindness as its horses.

st.rcm.ram_hurries_home.title: Ram hurries home
st.rcm.ram_hurries_home.lesson: When someone at home is waiting, no comfort elsewhere can hold you.
st.rcm.ram_hurries_home.summary: After the war, Vibhishan begs Ram to stay a while, bathe and rest in Lanka's palaces. Ram says all of it is his as much as Vibhishan's, but thinking of Bharat waiting at home, each moment feels like an age; if he is late, he may not find his brother alive.

st.rcm.bharat_last_day.title: The last day of waiting
st.rcm.bharat_last_day.lesson: Waiting is hardest on the last day; hope can arrive just as you go under.
st.rcm.bharat_last_day.summary: One day is left of the fourteen years and there is no word. Bharat wonders whether Ram has forgotten him, and his mind starts to sink. Just then Hanuman arrives like a boat and says Ram is coming. Bharat says no gift could repay this news.

st.rcm.angad_asks_to_stay.title: Ram says goodbye to his friends
st.rcm.angad_asks_to_stay.lesson: Friendships made in hard times deserve to be kept; say so out loud.
st.rcm.angad_asks_to_stay.summary: After six happy months, Ram sends his monkey and bear friends home with gifts. Angad, whose father is dead, begs to stay: Ram is his father and mother now. Ram embraces him and sends him on. To the boatman Guha he says: you are a brother to me; keep visiting.

st.rcm.ram_asks_to_be_corrected.title: Ram's address to the citizens
st.rcm.ram_asks_to_be_corrected.lesson: A good leader invites correction; a good life is simple, honest and free of grudges.
st.rcm.ram_asks_to_be_corrected.summary: Ram calls his people together and says he speaks without pride of rank: if he says anything wrong, stop him without fear. The way he recommends needs no grand effort, only a simple nature, an honest mind, contentment, and no grudges, no quarrels, no craving and no fear.

st.rcm.garuda_doubts_after_rescue.title: Garuda's doubt
st.rcm.garuda_doubts_after_rescue.lesson: Doubt is human; stay long enough in good company and it can lead somewhere better.
st.rcm.garuda_doubts_after_rescue.summary: Garuda, Vishnu's own mount, frees Ram from a serpent-noose in battle and starts to doubt: how can God be bound? He goes to Narada, Brahma and Shiva, who sends him to an old crow, Kakbhushundi, saying doubts clear only with long time in good company. Kakbhushundi tells him no one has escaped delusion, desire, craving or anger; Garuda ends up grateful for the doubt that led him there.

st.rcm.kakbhushundi_doubts_the_toddler.title: Kakbhushundi and the child Ram
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_doubts_the_toddler.lesson: Pride is taken from us painfully, for our good; what remains is what matters.
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_doubts_the_toddler.summary: Kakbhushundi used to visit Ayodhya to watch Ram as a child. Once he doubted that a toddler chasing a crow could be God; Ram reached for him across every world, and he saw universes inside the child's mouth. Humbled, he was offered every power and chose devotion, since comforts without it are a feast without salt. Ram explains that pride is lanced from those he loves, as a mother lances a child's boil.

st.rcm.student_who_would_not_rise.title: The student who would not stand for his teacher
st.rcm.student_who_would_not_rise.lesson: Respect those who teach you; and forgive like the teacher who prayed for his rude student.
st.rcm.student_who_would_not_rise.summary: In an earlier life Kakbhushundi was a proud, wealthy, sharp-tongued young man whose gentle teacher kept trying to guide him. One day in the temple he refused even to rise when the teacher entered. The teacher said nothing, but a curse fell on the student; the teacher at once prayed for him, asking that he not be punished in anger. Lives later, the one thorn Kakbhushundi still carries is the memory of that teacher's gentleness.

st.rcm.kakbhushundi_cursed_and_glad.title: Arguing with Lomash
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_cursed_and_glad.lesson: Even calm people burn when pushed too far; take correction without bitterness.
st.rcm.kakbhushundi_cursed_and_glad.summary: As a young seeker Kakbhushundi went to the sage Lomash, who taught the formless God; Kakbhushundi kept arguing for his own view until the sage, provoked again and again, lost his temper and cursed him to become a crow. Kakbhushundi took it without fear or self-pity, and the sage, regretting his anger, called him back and taught him the Ramcharitmanas.

st.rcm.manas_rog.title: Garuda's seven questions
st.rcm.manas_rog.lesson: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.
st.rcm.manas_rog.summary: Garuda asks seven questions: the rarest body, the greatest sorrow and joy, the nature of good and wicked people, the highest virtue and the worst wrong, and the diseases of the mind. Kakbhushundi answers: no sorrow like want, no joy like meeting good people; non-harm is highest and slander worst; delusion is the root disease, with lust, greed, anger, envy and ego as its symptoms.

st.rcm.lamp_and_the_gem.title: Kakbhushundi explains why the lamp of knowledge goes out and the gem of devotion does not
st.rcm.lamp_and_the_gem.lesson: Knowledge is a lamp the winds can put out; devotion is a gem that shines by itself.
st.rcm.lamp_and_the_gem.summary: Garuda asks the difference between knowledge and devotion. Kakbhushundi, who has walked both paths and was cursed for preferring one, answers with an image Garuda can hold.

st.rcm.tara_consoled.title: Ram consoles Tara
st.rcm.tara_consoled.lesson: Grief needs time; later, perspective on what is lost and what endures can comfort.
st.rcm.tara_consoled.summary: After Bali's death his wife Tara weeps over his body. Ram speaks to her gently: the body is made of five elements and lies here before her, but the self is not only this body; for whom is she weeping? Comforted, she asks for devotion, and Bali's son Angad is made heir.

st.bhakti.tulsi_turned_by_ratnavali.title: Tulsidas follows his wife across a flooded river and is turned by her words
st.bhakti.tulsi_turned_by_ratnavali.lesson: Intense love, redirected, can become devotion; a sharp word at the right moment can turn a life.
st.bhakti.tulsi_turned_by_ratnavali.summary: In the story the tradition tells, the young Tulsidas is so attached to his wife Ratnavali that when she goes to her father's house without him, he follows the same night, crossing a river in flood and climbing to her room. Embarrassed in front of her family, she speaks sharply.

st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child.title: Tulsidas, the boy who begged for scraps
st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child.lesson: Where you start is not where you end; you can be taken in from nothing.
st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child.summary: Across his later works Tulsidas tells his own story: left by his parents at birth, he wandered door to door for scraps, no job, no trade, no skill, ignored by everyone. Good people told him not to worry; Hanuman raised him like a child; Ram's name, he says, turned a thorny babul into a mango tree. Even when he went astray, he was taken back.

st.bhakti.tulsi_no_more_wasting.title: Tulsidas resolves: till now I wasted my life; I will not waste it any more
st.bhakti.tulsi_no_more_wasting.lesson: What was wasted is past; by grace one wakes, and can refuse to sleep again.
st.bhakti.tulsi_no_more_wasting.summary: Looking back on years lost to the pull of the senses, Tulsidas does not lament for long. He writes a song of waking up.

st.bhakti.tulsi_bahuk_pain_in_the_arm.title: Old Tulsidas, in unbearable pain, argues with Hanuman
st.bhakti.tulsi_bahuk_pain_in_the_arm.lesson: In pain one may complain openly to the one we trust; complaint and trust can live in the same breath.
st.bhakti.tulsi_bahuk_pain_in_the_arm.summary: Near the end of his life Tulsidas is struck by a fierce pain in his arm and body, in a Kashi swept by sickness. It does not let up day or night. He does not know whether it is time, karma, past sin or simply his constitution.

st.bhakti.tulsi_call_me_what_you_like.title: People call Tulsidas a rogue, a weaver, a Rajput; he does not argue
st.bhakti.tulsi_call_me_what_you_like.lesson: When you need nothing from your critics, their labels have nothing to hold on to.
st.bhakti.tulsi_call_me_what_you_like.summary: In Kashi, the learned and the orthodox talk about Tulsidas: who is he, what caste, what is he doing writing Ram's story in the common tongue? The labels pile up.

st.bhakti.meera_leaves_the_family_way.title: Meera refuses the life her royal family expects of her
st.bhakti.meera_leaves_the_family_way.lesson: When devotion is real, the world's labels and threats lose their grip; there is no second.
st.bhakti.meera_leaves_the_family_way.summary: Meera, married into the royal house of Mewar, will not live as a royal widow and daughter-in-law is expected to. She sings and dances before Krishna in temples, sits with sadhus, and says openly that Giridhar is her husband. Her in-laws are outraged.

st.bhakti.meera_no_one_knows_my_pain.title: Meera: only the wounded know the wounded
st.bhakti.meera_no_one_knows_my_pain.lesson: Only one who has been wounded understands the wound; the pain of longing for God is healed only by God.
st.bhakti.meera_no_one_knows_my_pain.summary: Meera is in the pain of separation and no one around her understands it. They think it strange, or a madness, or something to be talked out of.

st.bhakti.meera_found_the_jewel.title: Meera has found the jewel of Ram's name and wants nothing more
st.bhakti.meera_found_the_jewel.lesson: The wealth that grows when spent and cannot be stolen is the Name, received by grace.
st.bhakti.meera_found_the_jewel.summary: After a life of losses, Meera sings of something she has gained.

st.bhakti.sur_danced_enough.title: Surdas: I have danced enough, Gopal
st.bhakti.sur_danced_enough.lesson: Seen clearly, the life driven by craving is a costume dance; one can ask to stop.
st.bhakti.sur_danced_enough.summary: Surdas looks at his whole life as one long performance on a stage, dressed and made up by his own cravings.

st.bhakti.sur_stop_wailing.title: Surdas sings only of his own sins until his guru tells him to sing of Krishna
st.bhakti.sur_stop_wailing.lesson: Confession has its place; then stop wailing and sing of the One who turns iron to gold.
st.bhakti.sur_stop_wailing.summary: Surdas, a singer at Gau Ghat near Mathura, sings mostly of how sinful he is: who is as crooked, wicked and lustful as me? I forgot the one who gave me this body, I am a traitor to my salt, I run after the senses like a village pig.

st.bhakti.sur_krishna_misses_his_mother.title: Krishna, now a prince in Mathura, sends word home: no one here calls me Kanhaiya
st.bhakti.sur_krishna_misses_his_mother.lesson: Splendour abroad cannot replace being known by your childhood name at home.
st.bhakti.sur_krishna_misses_his_mother.summary: Krishna has left Gokul for Mathura. He has killed Kamsa, is honoured as a prince, and everything is splendid. He finds a traveller going toward Braj and gives him a message for the woman who raised him.

st.bhakti.sur_gajendra_calls_last.title: The elephant who finally called (as Surdas sings it)
st.bhakti.sur_gajendra_calls_last.lesson: Fight with everything you have; when your strength runs out, call. Help comes running.
st.bhakti.sur_gajendra_calls_last.summary: An elephant king is seized by a crocodile in a lake and struggles for a thousand years with all his strength and his herd. Only when his strength is gone does he call out to Hari, who leaves his mount behind and runs barefoot to free him. Surdas returns to the story again and again (vp.11, 21, 241, 256).

st.bhakti.kabir_looking_for_the_bad_one.title: Kabir goes looking for a bad person and finds himself
st.bhakti.kabir_looking_for_the_bad_one.lesson: Look for fault in your own heart first; keep the one who criticises you close.
st.bhakti.kabir_looking_for_the_bad_one.summary: Kabir, a weaver in Kashi who spoke plainly about everyone's hypocrisy, Hindu and Muslim alike, turns the same eye on himself.

st.bhakti.kabir_the_weavers_sheet.title: Kabir the weaver: the body is a fine sheet, to be returned unstained
st.bhakti.kabir_the_weavers_sheet.lesson: The body is lent cloth: wear it carefully, do your work now, and give it back clean.
st.bhakti.kabir_the_weavers_sheet.summary: Kabir earns his living at a loom. He sings about what he knows: thread, warp, weft and cloth.

st.bhakti.kabir_slowly_mind.title: Kabir to his own restless mind: slowly, slowly
st.bhakti.kabir_slowly_mind.lesson: Water faithfully; the fruit comes in its season, not because you poured more.
st.bhakti.kabir_slowly_mind.summary: The mind wants the result now. Kabir talks to it the way a gardener would.

st.bhakti.rahim_when_the_days_turn.title: Rahim, once the empire's great general, writes about the turning of days
st.bhakti.rahim_when_the_days_turn.lesson: Fortune turns; in the bad days stay quiet, learn who your friends are, and go where the exiled go.
st.bhakti.rahim_when_the_days_turn.summary: Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan was one of the most powerful men of Akbar's empire: commander, scholar, famously generous. Under Jahangir he fell out of favour; history records that he lost sons and position. In his dohas the man who had everything writes about losing it.

st.bhakti.rahim_lowered_eyes.title: Rahim gives with his eyes lowered, and explains why
st.bhakti.rahim_lowered_eyes.lesson: When you give, remember who the Giver is; that is why the eyes go down.
st.bhakti.rahim_lowered_eyes.summary: Rahim, as Khan-i-Khanan, was known for giving to anyone who came, and for doing it with his eyes cast down.

st.up.nachiketa_questions_father.title: Nachiketa questions his father's gift
st.up.nachiketa_questions_father.lesson: A child's honest question can show up an adult's empty gesture.
st.up.nachiketa_questions_father.summary: A father makes a show of giving away all he owns, but the cows are old and dry. His young son Nachiketa keeps asking who he will be given to, until the father snaps, 'To Death!' The boy goes, and tells his father to keep his word.

st.up.nachiketa_three_nights_first_boon.title: The three boons and the refused fortune
st.up.nachiketa_three_nights_first_boon.lesson: Ask for peace with your family first, and don't trade the real question for comfort.
st.up.nachiketa_three_nights_first_boon.summary: Death, away from home, keeps the boy waiting three days and offers three boons in apology. Nachiketa asks first that his father be calm and not angry with him, then for a sacred fire, then for the truth about death. Yama tempts him with sons, gold, long life and pleasures instead; the boy refuses them all.

st.up.nachiketa_refuses_bribes.title: The three boons and the refused fortune
st.up.nachiketa_refuses_bribes.lesson: Ask for peace with your family first, and don't trade the real question for comfort.
st.up.nachiketa_refuses_bribes.summary: Death, away from home, keeps the boy waiting three days and offers three boons in apology. Nachiketa asks first that his father be calm and not angry with him, then for a sacred fire, then for the truth about death. Yama tempts him with sons, gold, long life and pleasures instead; the boy refuses them all.

st.up.ushasti_famine.title: Ushasti eats a stranger's leftovers in a famine and refuses the water
st.up.ushasti_famine.lesson: In real need, taking what keeps you alive is no fall; taking more than that is.
st.up.ushasti_famine.summary: Hail has destroyed the crops of the Kurus. Ushasti, a learned man, is wandering with his wife and has nothing. He begs from a man eating a bowl of poor beans, who says these scraps are all he has.

st.up.mahidasa_illness.title: Mahidasa speaks to his illness
st.up.mahidasa_illness.lesson: A life seen as an offering has work still to complete, and that gives strength in illness.
st.up.mahidasa_illness.summary: A man who understands his whole life as one long offering falls ill. He does not pretend the illness is absent. He turns and addresses it.

st.up.satyakama_truth_about_birth.title: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
st.up.satyakama_truth_about_birth.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.
st.up.satyakama_truth_about_birth.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.

st.up.satyakama_four_hundred_cows.title: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
st.up.satyakama_four_hundred_cows.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.
st.up.satyakama_four_hundred_cows.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.

st.up.upakosala_passed_over.title: Upakosala is passed over while every other student graduates
st.up.upakosala_passed_over.lesson: Service that seemed unnoticed was noticed; what you tended will itself speak for you.
st.up.upakosala_passed_over.summary: Upakosala has tended his teacher's fires for twelve years. The teacher lets the other students go home, one after another, and says nothing to him. Then the teacher leaves on a journey. Upakosala stops eating.

st.up.shvetaketu_comes_home_proud.title: Shvetaketu comes home proud
st.up.shvetaketu_comes_home_proud.lesson: Learning without humility misses the main thing.
st.up.shvetaketu_comes_home_proud.summary: After twelve years of study, Shvetaketu returns home at twenty-four full of himself. His father gently asks whether he learned the one thing that makes everything else understood, and the son admits his teachers never taught it.

st.up.shvetaketu_fifteen_day_fast.title: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
st.up.shvetaketu_fifteen_day_fast.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.
st.up.shvetaketu_fifteen_day_fast.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'

st.up.tat_tvam_asi_seed_and_salt.title: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
st.up.tat_tvam_asi_seed_and_salt.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.
st.up.tat_tvam_asi_seed_and_salt.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'

st.up.man_from_gandhara.title: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
st.up.man_from_gandhara.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.
st.up.man_from_gandhara.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'

st.up.narada_knows_everything_still_grie.title: Narada: learned but sad
st.up.narada_knows_everything_still_grie.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.
st.up.narada_knows_everything_still_grie.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.

st.up.indra_virochana.title: Indra and Virochana with Prajapati
st.up.indra_virochana.lesson: Don't settle for the first comfortable answer; keep asking until it holds.
st.up.indra_virochana.summary: Indra of the gods and Virochana of the demons study with Prajapati for 32 years to learn the self. Shown their dressed-up reflections, both leave satisfied; Virochana goes home teaching that the body is everything. Indra stops halfway, sees the flaw, and keeps coming back for 101 years until he learns that the self is not the body.

st.up.senses_quarrel.title: The senses argue over who is greatest
st.up.senses_quarrel.lesson: The quiet one everyone relies on often matters most.
st.up.senses_quarrel.summary: Speech, sight, hearing and mind each claim to be the most important. Their father says the greatest is the one whose absence hurts the body most. Each leaves for a year and the body manages; when breath starts to leave, all the others are torn loose and beg it to stay.

st.up.shvetaketu_jaivali_five_questions.title: Shvetaketu humbled at the king's court
st.up.shvetaketu_jaivali_five_questions.lesson: A good parent admits what they don't know and goes on learning.
st.up.shvetaketu_jaivali_five_questions.summary: Shvetaketu boasts that his father has taught him everything, then cannot answer a single one of a king's five questions. He runs home and blames his father, who honestly admits he does not know either, and goes to the king himself, refusing wealth and asking only to learn.

st.up.five_householders_ashvapati.title: Five scholars go to King Ashvapati
st.up.five_householders_ashvapati.lesson: Point people to someone who knows more, and say plainly what you came for.
st.up.five_householders_ashvapati.summary: Five great scholars come to Uddalaka to learn. Knowing he cannot answer everything, he takes them to King Ashvapati instead. The king proudly says his kingdom has no thieves or drunkards and offers gifts, but the scholars politely insist on the purpose they came for.

st.up.first_being_afraid_alone.title: The first being: fear, loneliness and dharma
st.up.first_being_afraid_alone.lesson: Fear and loneliness are human; truth gives even the weak a footing.
st.up.first_being_afraid_alone.summary: In this creation story the first being, alone, feels fear, then realises there is no one else to fear. He feels no joy alone and longs for a companion, splitting into husband and wife. Finally dharma is created, the truth by which even the weak can stand up to the strong.

st.up.balaki_ajatashatru.title: The proud teacher who runs out of answers and becomes the student
st.up.balaki_ajatashatru.lesson: Running out of answers is where learning starts, if you can say so.
st.up.balaki_ajatashatru.summary: Balaki, learned and proud, walks into King Ajatashatru's court and announces, 'I will tell you about Brahman.' The king offers a thousand cows for the offer alone. Balaki gives twelve definitions, one after another. To each the king says, 'Do not speak to me of that. I already hold that.'

st.up.maitreyi_what_would_i_do_with_weal.title: Maitreyi refuses the inheritance
st.up.maitreyi_what_would_i_do_with_weal.lesson: Wealth buys comfort; ask for what lasts.
st.up.maitreyi_what_would_i_do_with_weal.summary: Before leaving home, Yajnavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asks whether all the world's wealth would make her immortal, and when he says no, she asks for what he knows instead. He teaches her that we love husband, wife and children for the self shining in them.

st.up.maitreyi_you_have_confused_me.title: Maitreyi refuses the inheritance
st.up.maitreyi_you_have_confused_me.lesson: Wealth buys comfort; ask for what lasts.
st.up.maitreyi_you_have_confused_me.summary: Before leaving home, Yajnavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asks whether all the world's wealth would make her immortal, and when he says no, she asks for what he knows instead. He teaches her that we love husband, wife and children for the self shining in them.

st.up.janaka_contest_yajnavalkya_cows.title: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
st.up.janaka_contest_yajnavalkya_cows.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.
st.up.janaka_contest_yajnavalkya_cows.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.

st.up.gargi_two_arrows.title: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
st.up.gargi_two_arrows.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.
st.up.gargi_two_arrows.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.

st.up.janaka_steps_down_from_throne.title: Janaka asks: what is our light?
st.up.janaka_steps_down_from_throne.lesson: When every outer light fails, you still have your own.
st.up.janaka_steps_down_from_throne.summary: Yajnavalkya asks the rich, learned King Janaka where he will go when he dies, and the king admits he does not know. Later Janaka asks what light a person lives by: sun, then moon, then fire, then voice, and when all are gone, the self is one's own light.

st.up.da_da_da.title: Da Da Da: the voice of thunder
st.up.da_da_da.lesson: Each of us hears the lesson we most need: restraint, generosity or compassion.
st.up.da_da_da.summary: Gods, humans and demons finish their studies with their father Prajapati and ask for a parting word. To each he says only 'Da'. The gods hear 'be self-controlled', humans hear 'give', and demons hear 'be compassionate'. The thunder still repeats it.

st.up.bhrigu_sent_back.title: Bhrigu learns from his father
st.up.bhrigu_sent_back.lesson: A wise parent lets a child discover the answer instead of handing it over.
st.up.bhrigu_sent_back.summary: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him what is ultimate. Varuna gives only a clue and tells him to reflect. Bhrigu comes back four times with answers (food, breath, mind, understanding) and each time is sent back to go deeper, until he discovers that everything is born from joy, lives by joy and returns to joy.

st.up.convocation_parting_words.title: The graduation address
st.up.convocation_parting_words.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.
st.up.convocation_parting_words.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.

st.up.kena_gods_and_yaksha.title: The gods take credit for a victory, and cannot burn a blade of grass
st.up.kena_gods_and_yaksha.lesson: The power by which you succeed is not of your own making.
st.up.kena_gods_and_yaksha.summary: Brahman wins a victory for the gods. The gods look at it and think, 'This victory is ours. This greatness is ours.' A strange being appears before them and they do not know what it is.

st.up.prashna_wait_a_year.title: Six seekers wait a year
st.up.prashna_wait_a_year.lesson: Readiness matters, and a good teacher only claims what he knows.
st.up.prashna_wait_a_year.summary: Six earnest seekers come to the sage Pippalada with questions. Instead of answering, he asks them to live with him for a year in discipline and faith, and only promises to answer what he actually knows.

st.up.sukesha_refuses_to_bluff.title: Sukesha refuses to bluff
st.up.sukesha_refuses_to_bluff.lesson: Saying 'I don't know' keeps you honest and keeps you learning.
st.up.sukesha_refuses_to_bluff.summary: A prince once asked Sukesha a hard question. Rather than bluff, Sukesha said 'I do not know,' because whoever lies withers to the root. The prince drove off in silence, and Sukesha carried the question to his teacher.

st.up.shaunaka_householder_asks.title: Shaunaka's question: two kinds of knowledge
st.up.shaunaka_householder_asks.lesson: Skills and degrees are real knowledge, but not the deepest kind.
st.up.shaunaka_householder_asks.summary: A wealthy householder asks a sage what single thing, once known, explains everything. Angiras says all our sciences and rituals are the lower knowledge; the higher is knowing the imperishable. He warns against people wise in their own eyes and sends the seeker to a real teacher.

st.up.two_birds.title: Two birds on one tree
st.up.two_birds.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.
st.up.two_birds.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.

st.up.chariot.title: The chariot of the self
st.up.chariot.lesson: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.
st.up.chariot.summary: Yama pictures a person as a chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. With a steady mind the horses obey; without it they bolt. He ends with the call to arise and wake.

st.up.father_and_son_back_to_school.title: Father and son go back to school
st.up.father_and_son_back_to_school.lesson: A parent who says 'let's learn together' teaches more than any answer.
st.up.father_and_son_back_to_school.summary: A patron asks young Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer. He asks his father, who admits he does not know either and suggests they both go to the patron as students. Chitra welcomes Uddalaka for his humility.

st.up.pratardana_you_choose.title: Pratardana is offered any boon and says, 'You choose what is best for me'
st.up.pratardana_you_choose.lesson: The best thing a person can ask for is to know the self.
st.up.pratardana_you_choose.summary: Pratardana, a king, reaches Indra's own dwelling by courage and by battle. Indra says, 'Choose a boon.' A warrior at the height of success could ask for anything.

st.up.fathers_last_handing_over.title: The father's last gift
st.up.fathers_last_handing_over.lesson: Parents pass on far more than property; they pass on themselves.
st.up.fathers_last_handing_over.summary: When a father feels death near, he lies down and his son lies over him, and they exchange words: the father places his speech, breath, sight, hearing, joys and sorrows in the son, and the son receives each one.

st.up.brihadratha_frog_in_dry_well.title: King Brihadratha's despair
st.up.brihadratha_frog_in_dry_well.lesson: Even success can leave you feeling stuck; asking for help is the first step out.
st.up.brihadratha_frog_in_dry_well.summary: A king hands his throne to his son and goes to the forest, overwhelmed by how everything decays. When a sage offers him a wish, he says he feels like a frog in a dark well and asks to be shown the way out.

st.up.shuka_at_janakas_gate.title: Shuka at Janaka's gate
st.up.shuka_at_janakas_gate.lesson: Steadiness is proved when neither neglect nor luxury moves you.
st.up.shuka_at_janakas_gate.summary: Young Shuka, already wise, is sent by his father Vyasa to King Janaka. Janaka ignores him at the gate for seven days, then lets him wait in the courtyard seven more, then surrounds him with luxury for seven days. Shuka stays exactly the same throughout, and Janaka bows to him.

st.up.nidagha_after_the_pilgrimage.title: Nidagha's lament
st.up.nidagha_after_the_pilgrimage.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.
st.up.nidagha_after_the_pilgrimage.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.

st.gitas.janaka_asks_ashtavakra.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
st.gitas.janaka_asks_ashtavakra.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.
st.gitas.janaka_asks_ashtavakra.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.

st.gitas.janaka_how_long_i_was_fooled.title: Janaka's astonished awakening
st.gitas.janaka_how_long_i_was_fooled.lesson: Seeing clearly can feel like waking up: nothing changed outside, everything changed inside.
st.gitas.janaka_how_long_i_was_fooled.summary: Hearing the first teaching, Janaka bursts into wonder: he sees he has been fooled by confusion for years. He describes owning nothing and everything, and losing his fear.

st.gitas.ashtavakra_tests_janaka.title: Ashtavakra tests the king
st.gitas.ashtavakra_tests_janaka.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.
st.gitas.ashtavakra_tests_janaka.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.

st.gitas.janaka_tired_of_doing.title: Janaka's songs of simple happiness
st.gitas.janaka_tired_of_doing.lesson: Happiness can be simple: do what comes, stop both grabbing and renouncing.
st.gitas.janaka_tired_of_doing.summary: In three short chapters Janaka describes how he has become calm: tired of busy body, speech and thought, he no longer renounces or grabs, and simply does what comes and lives happily.

st.gitas.avadhuta_why_do_you_weep.title: Why do you weep, friend?
st.gitas.avadhuta_why_do_you_weep.lesson: In grief, remember there is something in you that loss cannot touch.
st.gitas.avadhuta_why_do_you_weep.summary: In a long hymn with the refrain 'I am the nectar of knowledge, vast as the sky', Dattatreya asks a friend again and again why he weeps, since what he truly is does not age, die or change.

st.gitas.swan_on_insults.title: How the swan answers insults
st.gitas.swan_on_insults.lesson: When insulted, staying calm protects you more than hitting back.
st.gitas.swan_on_insults.summary: The swan teaches that words are arrows, that answering insult with insult only inflames both sides, and that the person who stays calm and wishes no harm sleeps in peace while the insulter carries the damage.

st.gitas.lakshmana_private_question.title: Lakshmana's private question
st.gitas.lakshmana_private_question.lesson: Even the closest companion needs to ask; with faith and guidance, you can become steady.
st.gitas.lakshmana_private_question.summary: After the war and his coronation, Rama is sitting alone when Lakshmana bows and asks how to cross the sea of confusion. Rama teaches him that knowledge, not ritual alone, frees a person, and that faith and a teacher make one steady as a mountain.

st.gitas.learned_seers_no_peace.title: Learned seers find no peace and go to Ganesha
st.gitas.learned_seers_no_peace.lesson: Learning alone may not settle the heart; turning to God can.
st.gitas.learned_seers_no_peace.summary: Seers who had received all the Vedas still found no peace, so they went to Ganesha's world and took refuge in him. Ganesha tells them that though he has no form, loving devotees see him in the form they long for, and that knowing his highest form brings lasting peace.

st.yv.rama_stops_eating_after_pilgrimage.title: Rama comes home from his pilgrimage and loses interest in everything
st.yv.rama_stops_eating_after_pilgrimage.lesson: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.
st.yv.rama_stops_eating_after_pilgrimage.summary: Sixteen-year-old Rama returns from a long pilgrimage and quietly withdraws: he stops eating properly, stops laughing, ignores his duties and sits alone. His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.

st.yv.rama_speaks_what_is_the_point.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
st.yv.rama_speaks_what_is_the_point.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
st.yv.rama_speaks_what_is_the_point.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.

st.yv.dasharatha_cannot_let_rama_go.title: Dasharatha: 'He is not yet sixteen. Take me instead'
st.yv.dasharatha_cannot_let_rama_go.lesson: Love wants to keep the child from every risk; dharma and trust sometimes ask it to let him go.
st.yv.dasharatha_cannot_let_rama_go.summary: Vishvamitra arrives and the king promises him anything. The sage asks for Rama, to guard his sacrifice against demons. The father who has just given his word feels the floor go.

st.yv.arishtanemi_asks_about_heaven.title: Offered heaven, King Arishtanemi asks what is wrong with it
st.yv.arishtanemi_asks_about_heaven.lesson: A prize that sets you comparing and then runs out is worth asking about before you accept it.
st.yv.arishtanemi_asks_about_heaven.summary: King Arishtanemi has handed the kingdom to his son and is practising austerities on a mountain. A messenger of the gods arrives with a chariot, music and attendants: Indra invites him to heaven as his reward.

st.yv.karunya_stops_acting.title: Karunya stops acting: knowledge and action as two wings
st.yv.karunya_stops_acting.lesson: Don't freeze while you wait to be sure. Understanding and action have to fly together.
st.yv.karunya_stops_acting.summary: A student asks the sage Agastya whether freedom comes from action or from knowledge. Agastya answers with a story: young Karunya, confused by two scriptures, simply stopped doing anything, and his father had to show him that understanding and action work together.

st.yv.vasishtha_effort_over_fate.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
st.yv.vasishtha_effort_over_fate.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.
st.yv.vasishtha_effort_over_fate.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.

st.yv.lila_fears_losing_her_husband.title: Queen Lila fears losing her husband
st.yv.lila_fears_losing_her_husband.lesson: Love brings the fear of loss; trying to control death only deepens the fear.
st.yv.lila_fears_losing_her_husband.summary: Queen Lila loves her husband so much that she cannot bear the thought of his death. The wise tell her that nothing wins immortality, so she prays to the goddess Sarasvati instead. When the king dies, Sarasvati begins to show her that life and death are not what they seem.

st.yv.karkati_needle.title: Karkati gets exactly the boon she asked for and it makes her smaller
st.yv.karkati_needle.lesson: A wish born of hunger shrinks the one who gets it; satisfaction comes when the hunger itself is seen through.
st.yv.karkati_needle.summary: Karkati is a huge rakshasi whose hunger nothing fills. She thinks: if I could eat everyone in the land in one breath I would be satisfied. She does a thousand years of austerity and asks to become a needle, an iron pin and a living disease, so she can enter and consume every being.

st.yv.man_who_beats_himself.title: The man in the great forest who beats himself and runs
st.yv.man_who_beats_himself.lesson: The mind strikes itself with its own imaginings and then flees the pain; inquiry, a steady look, ends it.
st.yv.man_who_beats_himself.summary: In a vast empty forest Vasishtha sees a man with a thousand arms. With all of them he is striking his own back with clubs, and then running in terror from the blows. He falls into a blind well, climbs out after a long time, beats himself again, runs into a thorn thicket, then into a cool plantain grove where he laughs for a while, and then starts again.

st.yv.three_princes_who_never_were.title: The nurse's tale of three princes, two unborn and one never conceived
st.yv.three_princes_who_never_were.lesson: Much of what the mind treats as solid is a story told on a story.
st.yv.three_princes_who_never_were.summary: A small boy asks his nurse for a story. She tells him: once there were three fine princes in a city that did not exist. Two were never born and the third was never conceived. They set out, rested under three trees of which two never grew and one had no seed, bathed in three rivers of which two were dry and one had no water, and came to a city yet to be built.

st.yv.lavana_lifetime_in_an_hour.title: King Lavana lives a whole life of poverty and loss in a few moments on his throne
st.yv.lavana_lifetime_in_an_hour.lesson: The mind can make a lifetime in a moment, and a moment of a lifetime.
st.yv.lavana_lifetime_in_an_hour.summary: A magician enters King Lavana's court and waves a peacock-feather wand. A horse is led in. The king stares at it, motionless, for a short while. When he comes to, shaking, he tells the court where he has been: carried off into a wilderness, starving, taken in by a poor forest family, married, a father, and years later, in a great drought, watching his children go hungry.

st.yv.shukra_follows_a_daydream.title: Shukra sits beside his meditating father and follows one glance for lifetimes
st.yv.shukra_follows_a_daydream.lesson: Mana eva manushyanam: the mind is the person; you go where your attention lives.
st.yv.shukra_follows_a_daydream.summary: Bhrigu is deep in meditation on a mountain. His young son Shukra sits beside him with nothing to do. An apsara crosses the sky. Shukra's mind goes after her, and keeps going.

st.yv.dama_vyala_kata.title: Three warriors who could not lose, until they learned to say 'I'
st.yv.dama_vyala_kata.lesson: Fear enters with 'I' and 'mine'; action free of self-concern is unshaken.
st.yv.dama_vyala_kata.summary: The demon king Shambara creates three generals, Dama, Vyala and Kata, with no sense of self at all. They do not think 'I may die' or 'I must win'. They simply fight, and the gods cannot stand before them.

st.up.raikva_janashruti.title: A generous king overhears two swans say a man under a cart outshines him
st.up.raikva_janashruti.lesson: Whatever good people do flows to the one who knows what he knows, as lesser throws of the dice are won by the highest throw.
st.up.raikva_janashruti.summary: Janashruti is known everywhere as a giver. He has rest houses built on every road so that people can eat from his kitchens. One night, lying on his roof, he hears two swans flying over. One warns the other not to fly too close to the light of so great a man. The other answers: 'Why speak of him as if he were Raikva, the man with the cart?'

st.up.artabhaga_take_my_hand.title: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
st.up.artabhaga_take_my_hand.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.
st.up.artabhaga_take_my_hand.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.

st.up.family_around_the_dying.title: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
st.up.family_around_the_dying.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.
st.up.family_around_the_dying.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'

st.up.accused_holds_the_hot_axe.title: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
st.up.accused_holds_the_hot_axe.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.
st.up.accused_holds_the_hot_axe.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'

st.up.dogs_chant_for_food.title: The dogs who chanted 'Om, let us eat'
st.up.dogs_chant_for_food.lesson: Chanting the highest words with only the stomach in mind turns worship into a request for food.
st.up.dogs_chant_for_food.summary: A student goes out to a quiet place by the water to recite the Veda. A white dog appears. Other dogs gather round it and say: 'Sir, sing food for us. We are hungry.' The white dog tells them to come back in the morning, and the student, curious, waits to watch.

st.up.shvetashvatara_who_governs_us.title: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
st.up.shvetashvatara_who_governs_us.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.
st.up.shvetashvatara_who_governs_us.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).

st.gitas.gods_grow_comfortable.title: Vishnu on where fear comes from
st.gitas.gods_grow_comfortable.lesson: Every gain brings its own fear; holding things lightly is the way out.
st.gitas.gods_grow_comfortable.summary: The frightened gods ask Vishnu how to become fearless. He explains that every possession carries its own fear (the body fears age, wealth fears thieves, power fears critics) and that only dispassion is free of fear; then he restates Bhagavad Gita 2.14-15 on enduring pleasure and pain.

st.gitas.ashtavakra_laughed_at_in_court.title: A boy bent in eight places walks into the king's court, and the court laughs
st.gitas.ashtavakra_laughed_at_in_court.lesson: A person is to be measured by what they know and are, not by age or body.
st.gitas.ashtavakra_laughed_at_in_court.summary: Ashtavakra was born with his body bent in eight places. As a boy of about twelve he learns that his father lost a debate at King Janaka's court to the scholar Bandi and was made to pay with his life. He walks to the palace. The gatekeeper will not let a child in.

st.yv.punya_consoles_pavana.title: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
st.yv.punya_consoles_pavana.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.
st.yv.punya_consoles_pavana.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.

st.yv.bali_same_days.title: Bali tires of endless days and asks his father's riddle
st.yv.bali_same_days.lesson: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.
st.yv.bali_same_days.summary: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day at his window he realises he is doing the same things day after day, night after night, and asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him: a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind; win it over, by practice, and everything is won.

st.yv.prahlada_refuge_in_victor.title: Prahlada, alone after defeat, takes refuge in Narayana
st.yv.prahlada_refuge_in_victor.lesson: Refuge is open to anyone, whatever their past; devotion kept up daily changes the mind.
st.yv.prahlada_refuge_in_victor.summary: With his father killed and his people beaten, the young demon prince Prahlada sees no way out except to take refuge in the very god he feared. He worships Vishnu in mind and in his shrine; the gods doubt a demon can be devoted, but Vishnu tells them he is ready. Vishnu appears, Prahlada sings a hymn of refuge, sinks into realisation and is gently woken to rule with a steady mind.

st.yv.prahlada_woken_to_rule.title: Prahlada: effort and grace are not rivals
st.yv.prahlada_woken_to_rule.lesson: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.
st.yv.prahlada_woken_to_rule.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Vasishtha answers that Prahlada earned it himself, that the Self and Vishnu are not two, and that sometimes we wake by our own effort and sometimes by grace reached through devotion. Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.

st.yv.uddalaka_restless_meditation.title: Young Uddalaka sits down to meditate and his mind will not stay
st.yv.uddalaka_restless_meditation.lesson: A restless mind is not overcome by force but by patient return and clear inquiry into what one is.
st.yv.uddalaka_restless_meditation.summary: Uddalaka is young, proud and serious. He longs for a calm mind: 'When will I rest in that stillness? When will my mind stop swinging between liking and disliking?' He sits in meditation in the forest, and his monkey-like mind runs to the objects of the senses.

st.yv.vitahavya_argues_with_his_mind.title: Vitahavya closes his eyes in a cave and finds his mind still talking
st.yv.vitahavya_argues_with_his_mind.lesson: The mind runs because it borrows life from awareness; seeing that, one stops obeying it.
st.yv.vitahavya_argues_with_his_mind.summary: The sage Vitahavya gives up his rituals and goes to a cave in the Vindhyas to sit still. He shuts his eyes and draws in his senses. His mind keeps going, jumping 'from pot to cloth to cart' like a leaf on the waves.

st.yv.suraghu_punish_or_pardon.title: King Suraghu cannot bear to punish, and cannot afford not to
st.yv.suraghu_punish_or_pardon.lesson: A ruler who must cause pain can act justly without being torn, by seeing that pain and pleasure arise in the mind and resting in the self.
st.yv.suraghu_punish_or_pardon.summary: Suraghu is a strong, fair king who rewards and punishes as his people deserve. But each punishment stays with him. 'Why do I crush the hearts of my people like sesame seeds in a press? They all feel pain.' He decides to stop, then sees that if he spares the wrongdoers, the good will be destroyed.

st.yv.bhasa_vilasa_old_friends.title: Two old friends meet again and admit they never found peace
st.yv.bhasa_vilasa_old_friends.lesson: Years of hard effort without inner understanding can leave you exactly where you started.
st.yv.bhasa_vilasa_old_friends.summary: Bhasa and Vilasa grow up inseparable in a forest hermitage. After their fathers die they drift apart and spend long lonely years in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, one asks if the other is well; he answers honestly that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries.

st.yv.janaka_overhears_the_siddhas.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
st.yv.janaka_overhears_the_siddhas.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
st.yv.janaka_overhears_the_siddhas.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.

st.yv.bhagiratha_begs_in_his_old_city.title: Bhagiratha gives away everything and goes begging in the city he once ruled
st.yv.bhagiratha_begs_in_his_old_city.lesson: Freedom is tested by standing without shame where one once stood in honour; the free person can rule or beg with the same mind.
st.yv.bhagiratha_begs_in_his_old_city.summary: Bhagiratha is a generous and capable king, yet he is tired of it all and finds his worldly life hollow. His teacher tells him that rank and possessions sit on top of the self; he must stand where the fear of poverty and the hunger for honour cannot reach.

st.yv.chudala_laughed_at_by_husband.title: Queen Chudala teaches her husband what renunciation really is
st.yv.chudala_laughed_at_by_husband.lesson: Running away doesn't free you; letting go inside does. Sometimes the teacher is the person beside you.
st.yv.chudala_laughed_at_by_husband.summary: Queen Chudala finds inner peace, but her husband, King Shikhidhvaja, doesn't believe her. Restless, he leaves his kingdom for the forest. Chudala rules wisely in his absence and visits him disguised as a young sage, Kumbha, who shows him that giving up kingdom, home and body is not renunciation; letting go of the clinging mind is. Freed, he returns home and rules beside her.

st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything.title: Queen Chudala teaches her husband what renunciation really is
st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything.lesson: Running away doesn't free you; letting go inside does. Sometimes the teacher is the person beside you.
st.yv.shikhidhvaja_burns_everything.summary: Queen Chudala finds inner peace, but her husband, King Shikhidhvaja, doesn't believe her. Restless, he leaves his kingdom for the forest. Chudala rules wisely in his absence and visits him disguised as a young sage, Kumbha, who shows him that giving up kingdom, home and body is not renunciation; letting go of the clinging mind is. Freed, he returns home and rules beside her.

st.yv.kacha_eight_years_no_peace.title: Kacha leaves home on his father's word, and after eight years asks why he is still not at peace
st.yv.kacha_eight_years_no_peace.lesson: The 'everything' that must be renounced is the mind itself, which holds all things.
st.yv.kacha_eight_years_no_peace.summary: Kacha, son of Brihaspati, is just leaving youth and asks his father how to be free. Brihaspati answers: by giving everything up. Kacha does exactly that, leaving home for the forest. His father grieves to see him go.

st.yv.bhushunda_the_old_crow.title: Bhushunda, the crow who outlived the ages
st.yv.bhushunda_the_old_crow.lesson: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.
st.yv.bhushunda_the_old_crow.summary: Vasishtha travels to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has watched world-ages come and go. Asked how he has lived so long, untroubled, Bhushunda lists his habits: he doesn't brood on the past or future, doesn't fret about what he'll get next, doesn't grow arrogant from knowing, and shares in others' joys and sorrows.

st.bh.fruit_passed_hand_to_hand.title: The fruit of immortality (legend of Bhartrihari's renunciation)
st.bh.fruit_passed_hand_to_hand.lesson: Betrayal can break you, or it can wake you up to what lasts.
st.bh.fruit_passed_hand_to_hand.summary: A legend, not history. A poor brahmin is given a fruit of immortality and, thinking a long life of poverty useless, gives it to King Bhartrihari of Ujjain. The king gives it to his beloved queen; it passes from lover to lover and returns to his hands. Heartbroken, he speaks 'yam cintayami' (Niti 2), hands the throne to his brother Vikrama and becomes a renunciant.

st.bh.forced_laughter_before_fools.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
st.bh.forced_laughter_before_fools.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.
st.bh.forced_laughter_before_fools.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.

st.bh.wrinkles_but_craving_young.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
st.bh.wrinkles_but_craving_young.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.
st.bh.wrinkles_but_craving_young.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.

st.bh.proud_man_asks_for_his_children.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of begging and servility
st.bh.proud_man_asks_for_his_children.lesson: Keep your dignity; ask for help for others before you ever grovel for yourself.
st.bh.proud_man_asks_for_his_children.summary: On the humiliation of begging favours from the rich: only hungry children could make a proud man ask. Contentment, not wealth, is real joy.

st.bh.three_kinds_of_people.title: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
st.bh.three_kinds_of_people.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.
st.bh.three_kinds_of_people.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.

st.bh.ascetic_and_king.title: Vairagyashatakam: Dialogue between the ascetic and the king
st.bh.ascetic_and_king.lesson: When the mind is content, nobody is richer than you.
st.bh.ascetic_and_king.summary: An ascetic tells a king who ignores him that learning equals wealth, that contentment in bark equals contentment in silk, and that pride over a few towns is a fever.

st.bh.house_of_many_then_one.title: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
st.bh.house_of_many_then_one.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.
st.bh.house_of_many_then_one.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.

st.bh.dog_and_elephant.title: Nitishatakam: Honour and spirit
st.bh.dog_and_elephant.lesson: Keep your dignity without needing to win every fight.
st.bh.dog_and_elephant.summary: Images of the lion and the elephant celebrate self-respect and inborn spirit. Some verses lean toward intolerance of insult, a warrior-king ideal.

st.viv.monkeys_of_varanasi.title: Chased by monkeys in Varanasi, he hears a stranger shout 'Face the brutes'
st.viv.monkeys_of_varanasi.lesson: The troubles we flee from chase us; when we turn and face them, they fall back.
st.viv.monkeys_of_varanasi.summary: In Varanasi he is walking a narrow way with a tank of water on one side and a high wall on the other. A troop of big, surly monkeys decide not to let him pass. They shriek, clutch at his feet and press closer. He starts to run, and the faster he runs, the faster they come, biting at him.

st.viv.frog_in_the_well.title: The frog in the well (Chicago, 15 September 1893)
st.viv.frog_in_the_well.lesson: Before you judge another faith or culture, check the size of your own well.
st.viv.frog_in_the_well.summary: Asked why religions quarrel, he tells of a frog who has lived all its life in a well. When a frog from the sea arrives and describes the ocean, the well-frog refuses to believe anything can be bigger than his well and drives the visitor out. Each of us, he says, sits in a little well and calls it the world.

st.viv.lion_among_sheep.title: A lion cub raised by sheep, who bleats and runs
st.viv.lion_among_sheep.lesson: We are not weak or sinful by nature; we have forgotten what we are, and one clear look can show it.
st.viv.lion_among_sheep.summary: A lioness dies leaping on a flock of sheep and gives birth as she falls. The cub is raised by the sheep. It eats grass and bleats. Grown huge, it still thinks it is a sheep and runs with the flock when danger comes.

st.viv.have_you_seen_god.title: A young man asks every preacher in Calcutta, 'Have you seen God?'
st.viv.have_you_seen_god.lesson: Religion is realisation; ask for the one who has seen, and keep asking until you find them.
st.viv.have_you_seen_god.summary: As a boy in Calcutta he goes from lecture to lecture in search of religion. He hears big talks. Afterwards he goes up to each speaker with one question: 'Have you seen God?'

st.viv.family_starving_or_the_mission.title: His father dies, the family is starving, and he is torn between them and his calling
st.viv.family_starving_or_the_mission.lesson: Great work is rarely done without a terrible inner struggle between love for one's own and the call one believes in.
