prasang:bg.p11.2.title: Krishna describes his cosmic form
prasang:bg.p11.2.lesson: Some truths need new eyes, not more effort.
prasang:bg.p11.2.summary: Krishna invites Arjuna to see countless forms and the whole universe in his body, and grants him divine eyes.

prasang:bg.p11.3.title: Sanjaya describes the cosmic form to Dhritarashtra
prasang:bg.p11.3.summary: Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra of a radiance brighter than a thousand suns and of Arjuna bowing in wonder.

prasang:bg.p11.4.title: Arjuna sees the cosmic form and praises it
prasang:bg.p11.4.lesson: Facing something vast can shake you to the core, and that's human.
prasang:bg.p11.4.summary: Arjuna sees all beings, gods and worlds in Krishna, and warriors rushing into his mouths like moths into flame. Terrified, he asks who Krishna really is.

prasang:bg.p11.5.title: "I am Time": Krishna urges Arjuna to fight
prasang:bg.p11.5.lesson: Do your part without imagining everything rests on you.
prasang:bg.p11.5.summary: Krishna declares he is Time, the destroyer of worlds; the warriors will die even without Arjuna, so he should rise and be the instrument.

prasang:bg.p11.6.title: Terrified, Arjuna prays to see the gentle four-armed form
prasang:bg.p11.6.lesson: We take those closest to us for granted; it is never too late to say sorry.
prasang:bg.p11.6.summary: Trembling, Arjuna praises Krishna, asks pardon for having treated him as just a friend, begs him to bear with him as a father, friend or lover would, and asks to see his familiar form.

prasang:bg.p11.7.title: Krishna returns to his gentle form
prasang:bg.p11.7.lesson: After the storm, kindness and a familiar face restore us.
prasang:bg.p11.7.summary: Krishna tells Arjuna not to fear, and returns to his familiar form to reassure him.

prasang:bg.p11.8.title: Only undivided devotion sees him
prasang:bg.p11.8.lesson: Hold no enmity towards any being.
prasang:bg.p11.8.summary: Arjuna is calm again. Krishna says no ritual or study reveals this form, only devotion, and the one free of attachment and enmity towards all reaches him.

prasang:bg.p12.1.title: Form or formless: which devotee is best, and the ways to reach him
prasang:bg.p12.1.lesson: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.
prasang:bg.p12.1.summary: Krishna says devotion to a personal form is easier, then offers a ladder: fix your mind; if not, practise; if not, work for me; if not, let go of results. Letting go brings peace at once.

prasang:bg.p12.2.title: The marks of one dear to God
prasang:bg.p12.2.lesson: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.
prasang:bg.p12.2.summary: Krishna lists the marks of one dear to him: no hatred, friendly and compassionate, forgiving, content, disturbing no one and disturbed by no one, the same in praise and blame.

prasang:bg.p13.1.title: The field and the knower of the field
prasang:bg.p13.1.lesson: Real knowledge shows up as character: humility, patience, honesty.
prasang:bg.p13.1.summary: Krishna calls the body the field and the self its knower, then lists what real knowledge looks like: humility, no pretence, patience, honesty, clear sight of ageing and illness.

prasang:bg.p13.2.title: Nature and spirit
prasang:bg.p13.2.lesson: See the same presence in everyone and you stop wounding yourself.
prasang:bg.p13.2.summary: Nature does the acting; the self witnesses. Some reach the truth by meditation, some by reason, some by work, some by listening. Whoever sees the same divine in all beings stops harming themselves.

prasang:bg.p14.1.title: The glory of knowledge; how nature and spirit give rise to the world
prasang:bg.p14.1.summary: Krishna calls nature the womb and himself the seed-giving father of all beings.

prasang:bg.p14.2.title: Sattva, rajas, tamas: the three gunas
prasang:bg.p14.2.lesson: Notice which mood is running you: clarity, restlessness or dullness.
prasang:bg.p14.2.summary: Sattva binds through attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas through craving and activity, tamas through laziness and sleep. Each shows itself in recognisable signs.

prasang:bg.p14.3.title: Going beyond the gunas
prasang:bg.p14.3.lesson: Let moods come and go without fighting or chasing them.
prasang:bg.p14.3.summary: One beyond the qualities does not hate moods when they come or long for them when they go, sits like a witness, and is the same in praise and blame, honour and insult.

prasang:bg.p15.1.title: The tree of worldly life, and the way out
prasang:bg.p15.1.lesson: Pride and clinging keep us tangled; detachment cuts through.
prasang:bg.p15.1.summary: The world is an ashvattha tree with roots above and branches below; cut it with detachment and seek the source. The free of pride and delusion reach it.

prasang:bg.p15.2.title: The individual soul
prasang:bg.p15.2.lesson: You are a part of something eternal.
prasang:bg.p15.2.summary: Each living being is an eternal part of Krishna, carrying mind and senses from body to body, seen only by the eye of wisdom.

prasang:bg.p15.3.title: The Supreme Lord and his power
prasang:bg.p15.3.lesson: The sacred is seated in every heart.
prasang:bg.p15.3.summary: Krishna is the light of sun and moon, the nourishment of plants, the digestive fire, and is seated in every heart.

prasang:bg.p15.4.title: The perishable, the imperishable and the Supreme Person
prasang:bg.p15.4.lesson: Beyond what changes and what lasts, there is more.
prasang:bg.p15.4.summary: Krishna distinguishes the perishable, the imperishable, and himself beyond both as the Supreme Person.

prasang:bg.p16.1.title: Divine and demonic qualities, and where they lead
prasang:bg.p16.1.lesson: Character is a list you can practise: courage, truth, kindness, no arrogance.
prasang:bg.p16.1.summary: Krishna lists the divine qualities (fearlessness, truth, no anger, compassion, forgiveness, humility) and the demonic ones (hypocrisy, arrogance, anger, harshness), and reassures Arjuna he has the good ones.

prasang:bg.p16.2.title: The demonic nature and its downfall
prasang:bg.p16.2.lesson: The mind of 'more' never rests; see it in yourself before it rules you.
prasang:bg.p16.2.summary: Krishna portrays people driven by endless desire and worry, bound by hundreds of hopes, always counting 'this I have, that I'll get', proud of wealth and birth.

prasang:bg.p16.3.title: Leave what scripture forbids; follow what it guides
prasang:bg.p16.3.lesson: Desire, anger, greed: close the three gates.
prasang:bg.p16.3.summary: Desire, anger and greed are the three gates to ruin; leaving them, one does what is truly good. Krishna points to scripture as a guide for what to do.

prasang:bg.p17.1.title: Faith, and harsh austerity against scripture
prasang:bg.p17.1.lesson: You become what you deeply believe.
prasang:bg.p17.1.summary: Everyone's faith matches their nature; a person is made of their faith. Harsh self-torment against scripture is condemned.

prasang:bg.p17.2.title: Three kinds of food, offering, austerity and giving
prasang:bg.p17.2.lesson: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.
prasang:bg.p17.2.summary: Food, offering, austerity and giving each come in three kinds. Speech should be true, kind and helpful; giving should expect nothing back; effort for show doesn't last.

prasang:bg.p17.3.title: The meaning of Om Tat Sat
prasang:bg.p17.3.summary: Om, Tat and Sat name the absolute; acts begun with them and done without wanting reward are good.

prasang:bg.p18.1.title: What true renunciation is
prasang:bg.p18.1.lesson: Don't drop what matters out of fear; drop the clinging instead.
prasang:bg.p18.1.summary: Krishna says good acts shouldn't be dropped; dropping duty out of fear or confusion gains nothing; real renunciation is giving up clinging to results, since no embodied being can stop acting.

prasang:bg.p18.2.title: What makes an action happen
prasang:bg.p18.2.lesson: You are one cause among five; own your part, not the whole outcome.
prasang:bg.p18.2.summary: Every action has five causes: the setting, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and providence. Seeing oneself as the only doer is a mistake.

prasang:bg.p18.3.title: Knowledge, action, doer, intellect, resolve and happiness by the three gunas
prasang:bg.p18.3.lesson: Choose the joy that's hard at first and sweet later.
prasang:bg.p18.3.summary: Krishna describes clear, restless and dull versions of action, doer, judgement, resolve and happiness: the best joy is poison first and nectar later; the restless kind is nectar first and poison later.

prasang:bg.p18.4.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang:bg.p18.4.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
prasang:bg.p18.4.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.

prasang:bg.p18.5.title: Established in knowledge
prasang:bg.p18.5.summary: Free of ego, force, arrogance, desire, anger and possessiveness, one becomes peaceful, neither grieving nor craving, the same to all.

prasang:bg.p18.6.title: Action with devotion: surrender
prasang:bg.p18.6.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.
prasang:bg.p18.6.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.

prasang:bg.p18.7.title: The glory of the Gita
prasang:bg.p18.7.lesson: Clarity, once found, turns into action.
prasang:bg.p18.7.summary: Krishna asks if Arjuna's confusion is gone; Arjuna says yes and that he will act. Sanjaya rejoices and declares that where Krishna and Arjuna stand, victory follows.

prasang:up.p.isha.whole.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang:up.p.isha.whole.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.
prasang:up.p.isha.whole.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.

prasang:up.p.katha.nachiketa_sent.title: Nachiketa questions his father's gift
prasang:up.p.katha.nachiketa_sent.lesson: A child's honest question can show up an adult's empty gesture.
prasang:up.p.katha.nachiketa_sent.summary: A father makes a show of giving away all he owns, but the cows are old and dry. His young son Nachiketa keeps asking who he will be given to, until the father snaps, 'To Death!' The boy goes, and tells his father to keep his word.

prasang:up.p.katha.three_boons.title: The three boons and the refused fortune
prasang:up.p.katha.three_boons.lesson: Ask for peace with your family first, and don't trade the real question for comfort.
prasang:up.p.katha.three_boons.summary: Death, away from home, keeps the boy waiting three days and offers three boons in apology. Nachiketa asks first that his father be calm and not angry with him, then for a sacred fire, then for the truth about death. Yama tempts him with sons, gold, long life and pleasures instead; the boy refuses them all.

prasang:up.p.katha.shreyas_preyas.title: The good and the pleasant
prasang:up.p.katha.shreyas_preyas.lesson: Every day offers a choice between what feels good and what is good.
prasang:up.p.katha.shreyas_preyas.summary: Yama praises Nachiketa for choosing the good over the pleasant. He explains that both come to every person, and the wise tell them apart, while the foolish choose what is pleasant and lose their way.

prasang:up.p.katha.deathless_self.title: Yama on what does not die
prasang:up.p.katha.deathless_self.lesson: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.
prasang:up.p.katha.deathless_self.summary: Death himself explains that the true self is never born and never dies, and is not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.

prasang:up.p.katha.chariot.title: The chariot of the self
prasang:up.p.katha.chariot.lesson: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.
prasang:up.p.katha.chariot.summary: Yama pictures a person as a chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. With a steady mind the horses obey; without it they bolt. He ends with the call to arise and wake.

prasang:up.p.katha.inward.title: Turning the gaze inward
prasang:up.p.katha.inward.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.
prasang:up.p.katha.inward.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.

prasang:up.p.mundaka.two_knowledges.title: Shaunaka's question: two kinds of knowledge
prasang:up.p.mundaka.two_knowledges.lesson: Skills and degrees are real knowledge, but not the deepest kind.
prasang:up.p.mundaka.two_knowledges.summary: A wealthy householder asks a sage what single thing, once known, explains everything. Angiras says all our sciences and rituals are the lower knowledge; the higher is knowing the imperishable. He warns against people wise in their own eyes and sends the seeker to a real teacher.

prasang:up.p.mundaka.bow.title: The archer and the target
prasang:up.p.mundaka.bow.lesson: Single-pointed attention is how anything worthwhile is reached.
prasang:up.p.mundaka.bow.summary: Angiras compares inner practice to archery: take the bow, set the arrow, draw with full attention and hit the target without distraction. When the highest is seen, the heart's knot loosens and doubts are cut.

prasang:up.p.mundaka.two_birds.title: Two birds on one tree
prasang:up.p.mundaka.two_birds.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.
prasang:up.p.mundaka.two_birds.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.

prasang:up.p.prashna.year.title: Six seekers wait a year
prasang:up.p.prashna.year.lesson: Readiness matters, and a good teacher only claims what he knows.
prasang:up.p.prashna.year.summary: Six earnest seekers come to the sage Pippalada with questions. Instead of answering, he asks them to live with him for a year in discipline and faith, and only promises to answer what he actually knows.

prasang:up.p.prashna.sukesha.title: Sukesha refuses to bluff
prasang:up.p.prashna.sukesha.lesson: Saying 'I don't know' keeps you honest and keeps you learning.
prasang:up.p.prashna.sukesha.summary: A prince once asked Sukesha a hard question. Rather than bluff, Sukesha said 'I do not know,' because whoever lies withers to the root. The prince drove off in silence, and Sukesha carried the question to his teacher.

prasang:up.p.taittiriya.convocation.title: The graduation address
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.convocation.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.convocation.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.

prasang:up.p.taittiriya.joy.title: The measure of joy
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.joy.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.joy.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.

prasang:up.p.taittiriya.bhrigu.title: Bhrigu learns from his father
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.bhrigu.lesson: A wise parent lets a child discover the answer instead of handing it over.
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.bhrigu.summary: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him what is ultimate. Varuna gives only a clue and tells him to reflect. Bhrigu comes back four times with answers (food, breath, mind, understanding) and each time is sent back to go deeper, until he discovers that everything is born from joy, lives by joy and returns to joy.

prasang:up.p.taittiriya.food.title: Vows of food and hospitality
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.food.lesson: Respect food and keep your door open.
prasang:up.p.taittiriya.food.summary: After Bhrigu's discovery come simple household vows: never speak ill of food, never waste it, make it plentiful, and turn no one away from your door.

prasang:up.p.aitareya.three_births.title: The three births of a person
prasang:up.p.aitareya.three_births.lesson: Care for the one who carries and raises the child; raising children continues your life.
prasang:up.p.aitareya.three_births.summary: The Aitareya describes three births: conception and pregnancy, when the mother nourishes the child and must herself be nourished; birth and upbringing, when caring for the child is caring for oneself; and death, when the parent, duties done, departs and the child carries on.

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.satyakama.title: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.satyakama.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.satyakama.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.senses_quarrel.title: The senses argue over who is greatest
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.senses_quarrel.lesson: The quiet one everyone relies on often matters most.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.senses_quarrel.summary: Speech, sight, hearing and mind each claim to be the most important. Their father says the greatest is the one whose absence hurts the body most. Each leaves for a year and the body manages; when breath starts to leave, all the others are torn loose and beg it to stay.

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.jaivali.title: Shvetaketu humbled at the king's court
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.jaivali.lesson: A good parent admits what they don't know and goes on learning.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.jaivali.summary: Shvetaketu boasts that his father has taught him everything, then cannot answer a single one of a king's five questions. He runs home and blames his father, who honestly admits he does not know either, and goes to the king himself, refusing wealth and asking only to learn.

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.ashvapati.title: Five scholars go to King Ashvapati
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.ashvapati.lesson: Point people to someone who knows more, and say plainly what you came for.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.ashvapati.summary: Five great scholars come to Uddalaka to learn. Knowing he cannot answer everything, he takes them to King Ashvapati instead. The king proudly says his kingdom has no thieves or drunkards and offers gifts, but the scholars politely insist on the purpose they came for.

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.shvetaketu_retur.title: Shvetaketu comes home proud
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.shvetaketu_retur.lesson: Learning without humility misses the main thing.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.shvetaketu_retur.summary: After twelve years of study, Shvetaketu returns home at twenty-four full of himself. His father gently asks whether he learned the one thing that makes everything else understood, and the son admits his teachers never taught it.

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.uddalaka_lessons.title: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.uddalaka_lessons.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.uddalaka_lessons.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.narada.title: Narada: learned but sad
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.narada.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.narada.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.

prasang:up.p.chhandogya.indra_virochana.title: Indra and Virochana with Prajapati
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.indra_virochana.lesson: Don't settle for the first comfortable answer; keep asking until it holds.
prasang:up.p.chhandogya.indra_virochana.summary: Indra of the gods and Virochana of the demons study with Prajapati for 32 years to learn the self. Shown their dressed-up reflections, both leave satisfied; Virochana goes home teaching that the body is everything. Indra stops halfway, sees the flaw, and keeps coming back for 101 years until he learns that the self is not the body.

prasang:up.p.brihad.first_being.title: The first being: fear, loneliness and dharma
prasang:up.p.brihad.first_being.lesson: Fear and loneliness are human; truth gives even the weak a footing.
prasang:up.p.brihad.first_being.summary: In this creation story the first being, alone, feels fear, then realises there is no one else to fear. He feels no joy alone and longs for a companion, splitting into husband and wife. Finally dharma is created, the truth by which even the weak can stand up to the strong.

prasang:up.p.brihad.maitreyi.title: Maitreyi refuses the inheritance
prasang:up.p.brihad.maitreyi.lesson: Wealth buys comfort; ask for what lasts.
prasang:up.p.brihad.maitreyi.summary: Before leaving home, Yajnavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asks whether all the world's wealth would make her immortal, and when he says no, she asks for what he knows instead. He teaches her that we love husband, wife and children for the self shining in them.

prasang:up.p.brihad.gargi.title: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
prasang:up.p.brihad.gargi.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.
prasang:up.p.brihad.gargi.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.

prasang:up.p.brihad.janaka.title: Janaka asks: what is our light?
prasang:up.p.brihad.janaka.lesson: When every outer light fails, you still have your own.
prasang:up.p.brihad.janaka.summary: Yajnavalkya asks the rich, learned King Janaka where he will go when he dies, and the king admits he does not know. Later Janaka asks what light a person lives by: sun, then moon, then fire, then voice, and when all are gone, the self is one's own light.

prasang:up.p.brihad.desire.title: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang:up.p.brihad.desire.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.
prasang:up.p.brihad.desire.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.

prasang:up.p.brihad.da_da_da.title: Da Da Da: the voice of thunder
prasang:up.p.brihad.da_da_da.lesson: Each of us hears the lesson we most need: restraint, generosity or compassion.
prasang:up.p.brihad.da_da_da.summary: Gods, humans and demons finish their studies with their father Prajapati and ask for a parting word. To each he says only 'Da'. The gods hear 'be self-controlled', humans hear 'give', and demons hear 'be compassionate'. The thunder still repeats it.

prasang:up.p.kaushitaki.father_son.title: Father and son go back to school
prasang:up.p.kaushitaki.father_son.lesson: A parent who says 'let's learn together' teaches more than any answer.
prasang:up.p.kaushitaki.father_son.summary: A patron asks young Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer. He asks his father, who admits he does not know either and suggests they both go to the patron as students. Chitra welcomes Uddalaka for his humility.

prasang:up.p.kaushitaki.bequest.title: The father's last gift
prasang:up.p.kaushitaki.bequest.lesson: Parents pass on far more than property; they pass on themselves.
prasang:up.p.kaushitaki.bequest.summary: When a father feels death near, he lies down and his son lies over him, and they exchange words: the father places his speech, breath, sight, hearing, joys and sorrows in the son, and the son receives each one.

prasang:up.p.maitrayani.brihadratha.title: King Brihadratha's despair
prasang:up.p.maitrayani.brihadratha.lesson: Even success can leave you feeling stuck; asking for help is the first step out.
prasang:up.p.maitrayani.brihadratha.summary: A king hands his throne to his son and goes to the forest, overwhelmed by how everything decays. When a sage offers him a wish, he says he feels like a frog in a dark well and asks to be shown the way out.

prasang:up.p.maitrayani.mind.title: The mind is your world
prasang:up.p.maitrayani.mind.lesson: Tend your mind; it decides whether you feel trapped or free.
prasang:up.p.maitrayani.mind.summary: The sage's verses on the mind: it is the world we live in, we become what it dwells on, and it alone binds or frees us depending on what it clings to.

prasang:up.p.maha.shuka.title: Shuka at Janaka's gate
prasang:up.p.maha.shuka.lesson: Steadiness is proved when neither neglect nor luxury moves you.
prasang:up.p.maha.shuka.summary: Young Shuka, already wise, is sent by his father Vyasa to King Janaka. Janaka ignores him at the gate for seven days, then lets him wait in the courtyard seven more, then surrounds him with luxury for seven days. Shuka stays exactly the same throughout, and Janaka bows to him.

prasang:up.p.maha.nidagha.title: Nidagha's lament
prasang:up.p.maha.nidagha.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.
prasang:up.p.maha.nidagha.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.

prasang:up.p.maha.ribhu_calm.title: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang:up.p.maha.ribhu_calm.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.
prasang:up.p.maha.ribhu_calm.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.

prasang:up.p.maha.ribhu_living.title: How a free person lives
prasang:up.p.maha.ribhu_living.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.
prasang:up.p.maha.ribhu_living.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.frame.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang:ashtavakra.p.frame.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.frame.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.janaka_awakens.title: Janaka's astonished awakening
prasang:ashtavakra.p.janaka_awakens.lesson: Seeing clearly can feel like waking up: nothing changed outside, everything changed inside.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.janaka_awakens.summary: Hearing the first teaching, Janaka bursts into wonder: he sees he has been fooled by confusion for years. He describes owning nothing and everything, and losing his fear.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.test.title: Ashtavakra tests the king
prasang:ashtavakra.p.test.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.test.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.bondage_freedom.title: What bondage and freedom really are
prasang:ashtavakra.p.bondage_freedom.lesson: Freedom is not elsewhere; it is a mind that stops grabbing and pushing away.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.bondage_freedom.summary: In four verses Ashtavakra defines bondage as a mind that wants, grieves, grabs, rejects, delights and rages, and freedom as a mind that stops doing so. Where 'I' takes over, there is bondage.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.detachment.title: The list that never ends
prasang:ashtavakra.p.detachment.lesson: The to-do list and life's ups and downs never end; peace comes from loosening your grip.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.detachment.summary: Ashtavakra points out that the pairs of done and undone, gain and loss, never end for anyone at any age, and that even sages disagree endlessly. Seeing this, one can stop fighting life and take what comes.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.craving.title: Craving is the treadmill
prasang:ashtavakra.p.craving.lesson: More money, pleasure or achievement won't give the mind rest; easing craving will.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.craving.summary: Ashtavakra tells Janaka that wherever craving lives, the endless round runs, and that wealth, pleasure and even good deeds have never given the mind rest. After so much toil, he says, it is time to stop.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.wisdom.title: The certainties of the calm
prasang:ashtavakra.p.wisdom.lesson: Most suffering is made of worry; knowing what you can't control loosens it.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.wisdom.summary: Ashtavakra lists convictions that make a person calm: things arise and pass by nature, fortune and misfortune come in their time, and suffering is born of worry alone.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.janaka_happiness.title: Janaka's songs of simple happiness
prasang:ashtavakra.p.janaka_happiness.lesson: Happiness can be simple: do what comes, stop both grabbing and renouncing.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.janaka_happiness.summary: In three short chapters Janaka describes how he has become calm: tired of busy body, speech and thought, he no longer renounces or grabs, and simply does what comes and lives happily.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.self_knowledge.title: You are not your mind
prasang:ashtavakra.p.self_knowledge.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.self_knowledge.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.special_instruction.title: Why striving and study do not bring peace
prasang:ashtavakra.p.special_instruction.lesson: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.special_instruction.summary: Ashtavakra warns that reading scriptures, working or meditating will not bring peace on their own; everyone suffers from straining, and running away from the world doesn't end pain. Even pride in being free is just more suffering.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.true_knower.title: Portrait of the one who knows
prasang:ashtavakra.p.true_knower.lesson: Contentment looks like not replaying the past or chasing the next thing.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.true_knower.summary: Ashtavakra describes the person who has understood: content alone, not replaying old pleasures or craving new ones, living happily on whatever comes, unmoved by praise or blame.

prasang:ashtavakra.p.peace.title: The calm of the wise
prasang:ashtavakra.p.peace.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.
prasang:ashtavakra.p.peace.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.

prasang:avadhuta.p.song_to_the_mind.title: Dattatreya's song to his own mind
prasang:avadhuta.p.song_to_the_mind.lesson: Talk to your restless mind like a friend: why all this chatter?
prasang:avadhuta.p.song_to_the_mind.summary: The wandering sage Dattatreya sings of the one Self and repeatedly turns to scold his own mind: why run around like a ghost, why all this chatter? You are vast as the sky.

prasang:avadhuta.p.take_the_essence.title: Take the jewel from the mud
prasang:avadhuta.p.take_the_essence.lesson: Wisdom matters more than who says it or how polished it sounds.
prasang:avadhuta.p.take_the_essence.summary: Dattatreya opens by saying wisdom should be taken from any teacher, however humble, and that plain words carry you across like an unpainted boat. He then describes thoughts as passing bubbles and the steady person who works for the good of all.

prasang:avadhuta.p.why_weep.title: Why do you weep, friend?
prasang:avadhuta.p.why_weep.lesson: In grief, remember there is something in you that loss cannot touch.
prasang:avadhuta.p.why_weep.summary: In a long hymn with the refrain 'I am the nectar of knowledge, vast as the sky', Dattatreya asks a friend again and again why he weeps, since what he truly is does not age, die or change.

prasang:avadhuta.p.marks_of_avadhuta.title: The marks of a free person
prasang:avadhuta.p.marks_of_avadhuta.lesson: A free person seeks no honour, gives it freely, and lives in the present.
prasang:avadhuta.p.marks_of_avadhuta.summary: The last chapter portrays the free sage as gentle, moderate, humble yet respectful to others, kind and truthful. Dattatreya then reads each syllable of 'A-va-dhu-ta' as a mark: free of expectation, living in the present, free of ego.

prasang:ram_gita.p.lakshman_asks.title: Lakshmana's private question
prasang:ram_gita.p.lakshman_asks.lesson: Even the closest companion needs to ask; with faith and guidance, you can become steady.
prasang:ram_gita.p.lakshman_asks.summary: After the war and his coronation, Rama is sitting alone when Lakshmana bows and asks how to cross the sea of confusion. Rama teaches him that knowledge, not ritual alone, frees a person, and that faith and a teacher make one steady as a mountain.

prasang:ram_gita.p.rope_and_snake.title: The rope and the snake
prasang:ram_gita.p.rope_and_snake.lesson: Much of our fear is a rope mistaken for a snake; look again.
prasang:ram_gita.p.rope_and_snake.summary: Rama explains that the Self is never born and never dies, that suffering comes from mistaking one thing for another like a rope for a snake, and that in deep sleep, free of wanting, we simply feel happy.

prasang:ram_gita.p.meditation_and_devoti.title: Sit quietly, keep faith
prasang:ram_gita.p.meditation_and_devoti.lesson: Quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural.
prasang:ram_gita.p.meditation_and_devoti.summary: Rama describes sitting in a quiet place with the senses at rest until the mind becomes like a still ocean, and tells Lakshmana that until he sees the divine everywhere, devotion keeps it alive in the heart.

prasang:hans_gita.p.swan_and_sadhyas.title: The golden swan and the Sadhyas
prasang:hans_gita.p.swan_and_sadhyas.lesson: Self-control, calm under insult and truth are the best way to live.
prasang:hans_gita.p.swan_and_sadhyas.summary: On his bed of arrows, Bhishma answers Yudhishthira's question about truth, self-control and forgiveness with an old story: the creator, in the form of a golden swan, met the Sadhya gods and taught them that self-control, calm under insult, truth and good company are the best way to live.

prasang:hans_gita.p.insults.title: How the swan answers insults
prasang:hans_gita.p.insults.lesson: When insulted, staying calm protects you more than hitting back.
prasang:hans_gita.p.insults.summary: The swan teaches that words are arrows, that answering insult with insult only inflames both sides, and that the person who stays calm and wishes no harm sleeps in peace while the insulter carries the damage.

prasang:hans_gita.p.questions.title: The Sadhyas' last questions
prasang:hans_gita.p.questions.lesson: Envy and greed quietly cost us our light and our friends.
prasang:hans_gita.p.questions.summary: Asked what covers the world and why people lose friends, the swan answers: ignorance covers it, envy dims it, greed costs friendships. The wise alone can be content, quiet in a crowd and free of quarrels.

prasang:vishnu_gita.p.roots_of_fear.title: Vishnu on where fear comes from
prasang:vishnu_gita.p.roots_of_fear.lesson: Every gain brings its own fear; holding things lightly is the way out.
prasang:vishnu_gita.p.roots_of_fear.summary: The frightened gods ask Vishnu how to become fearless. He explains that every possession carries its own fear (the body fears age, wealth fears thieves, power fears critics) and that only dispassion is free of fear; then he restates Bhagavad Gita 2.14-15 on enduring pleasure and pain.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.33.title: Vidura Niti: the wise and the fool
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.33.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.33.summary: Sleepless before the peace talks, King Dhritarashtra calls his half-brother Vidura for counsel. Vidura describes the marks of the wise and the fool, the faults that block progress, and the six joys of life.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.34.title: Vidura Niti: careful action and wounding words
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.34.lesson: Think before acting; if you did it right and it failed, don't sink. Guard your tongue.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.34.summary: Vidura continues through the night: weigh an action before you start it, don't sink when honest effort fails, and remember that words wound deeper than axes.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.35.title: Vidura Niti: Keshini's choice and the tests of character
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.35.lesson: Character shows under pressure. Do by day what will let you sleep at night.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.35.summary: Vidura tells how Prahlada judged honestly against his own son when Princess Keshini set two suitors a test, then gives aphorisms: gold is tested by fire, friends by hard times, and a clear conscience lets you sleep.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.36.title: Vidura Niti: Atreya and the Sadhyas, on insult and anger
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.36.lesson: When insulted, don't insult back. Swallow anger, and stand with your own people.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.36.summary: Vidura retells the sage Atreya's answer to the gods: don't insult back, hold your tongue, choose your company. He adds that anger is a bitter drink and that kin who stand together survive storms.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.37.title: Vidura Niti: what cuts life short
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.37.lesson: Arrogance, anger and betrayal shorten a life. Rivals in a family often protect each other.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.37.summary: Vidura lists Manu's seventeen kinds of fool and the six habits, from arrogance to betraying friends, that shorten a life more surely than death. He warns that the cousins need each other like a forest and its tigers.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.38.title: Vidura Niti: trust, secrecy and quarrels
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.38.lesson: Let results speak before announcements do.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.38.summary: Vidura speaks of welcoming guests, keeping plans private until done, whom to trust, and how quarrels with the powerful end.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.39.title: Vidura Niti: timing, gain and loss
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.39.lesson: Speak at the right time, weigh gain against cost, and repeat what is good until it becomes you.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.39.summary: Vidura teaches that good words land only at the right moment, that some gains are losses, that habits shape a person, and what people look for in a friend.

prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.40.title: Vidura Niti: never abandon what is right
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.40.lesson: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.
prasang:mbh.p.vidura_niti.40.summary: Vidura closes with the heart of his counsel: never give up what is right for desire, fear or greed; only our deeds go with us; ask the wise when unsure.

prasang:mbh.p.sanatsujatiya.title: Sanatsujatiya: the sage on death and the self
prasang:mbh.p.sanatsujatiya.lesson: Carelessness is the real death. Stay awake to your life and be who you are.
prasang:mbh.p.sanatsujatiya.summary: At Vidura's request the ancient sage Sanatsujata answers Dhritarashtra's fear of death. Death, he says, is heedlessness; desire drags us down; pretending to be what we are not is self-theft.

prasang:mbh.p.sanjaya_counsel.title: Sanjaya's plea for peace
prasang:mbh.p.sanjaya_counsel.lesson: No victory exempts you from old age, grief and death. Count what winning will cost.
prasang:mbh.p.sanjaya_counsel.summary: Dhritarashtra's envoy Sanjaya begs Yudhishthira not to fight for a kingdom: life is short, and no conquest saves anyone from age, loss or death.

prasang:mbh.p.yudhishthira_peace_case.title: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang:mbh.p.yudhishthira_peace_case.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.
prasang:mbh.p.yudhishthira_peace_case.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.

prasang:mbh.p.krishna_peace_embassy.title: Krishna's peace embassy to the Kauravas
prasang:mbh.p.krishna_peace_embassy.lesson: You can make the best case for peace and still be refused. Speak anyway.
prasang:mbh.p.krishna_peace_embassy.summary: Krishna travels to Hastinapura to plead for peace between the cousins. Elders, sages and finally Gandhari urge Duryodhana to share the kingdom; he refuses, even plotting to seize Krishna, and war becomes certain.

prasang:mbh.p.gandhari_counsel.title: Gandhari counsels her son
prasang:mbh.p.gandhari_counsel.lesson: Master yourself first. Greed never made anyone rich, and indulgent parents share the blame.
prasang:mbh.p.gandhari_counsel.summary: Summoned to the court, Queen Gandhari first blames her husband for indulging their son, then tells Duryodhana that whoever cannot rule himself cannot rule a kingdom, and that half the earth is enough.

prasang:mbh.p.vidula.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang:mbh.p.vidula.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.
prasang:mbh.p.vidula.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.

prasang:mbh.p.kshama_or_tejas.title: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang:mbh.p.kshama_or_tejas.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
prasang:mbh.p.kshama_or_tejas.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.

prasang:mbh.p.dharma_and_effort.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang:mbh.p.dharma_and_effort.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.
prasang:mbh.p.dharma_and_effort.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.

prasang:mbh.p.bhima_hanuman.title: Bhima meets Hanuman
prasang:mbh.p.bhima_hanuman.lesson: Strength without humility is blind. The one blocking your path may be family.
prasang:mbh.p.bhima_hanuman.summary: Searching for a flower for Draupadi, mighty Bhima finds an old monkey blocking the path and orders it to move. Told to lift its tail himself, he cannot budge it. The monkey is his elder brother Hanuman, who embraces him and teaches him.

prasang:mbh.p.ashtavakra.title: Ashtavakra at Janaka's court
prasang:mbh.p.ashtavakra.lesson: Age and appearance don't measure wisdom. Don't dismiss anyone for being young.
prasang:mbh.p.ashtavakra.summary: Ashtavakra, born bent in eight places by his father's curse, learns at twelve that his father drowned after losing a debate to the court sage Bandi. Turned away at the gate as a child, he argues his way in and defeats Bandi.

prasang:mbh.p.shibi_dove.title: King Shibi and the dove
prasang:mbh.p.shibi_dove.lesson: When duties collide, weigh them honestly, and keep your word to those who trust you.
prasang:mbh.p.shibi_dove.summary: A frightened dove flies to King Shibi for refuge; a hawk demands it back as its rightful food. Shibi offers the hawk anything else, finally his own flesh weighed against the dove, and climbs onto the scale himself. The birds reveal themselves as gods.

prasang:mbh.p.nahusha.title: Nahusha the python and Yudhishthira's answers
prasang:mbh.p.nahusha.lesson: Success can blind anyone. What makes a person good is conduct, not birth.
prasang:mbh.p.nahusha.summary: A giant python seizes Bhima. It is King Nahusha, once lord of heaven, cursed for making sages carry his palanquin. He frees Bhima after Yudhishthira answers his questions on goodness, and is freed himself.

prasang:mbh.p.draupadi_satyabhama.title: Draupadi and Satyabhama on marriage
prasang:mbh.p.draupadi_satyabhama.lesson: Love can't be managed or manipulated into place; trust grows only where no one feels controlled.
prasang:mbh.p.draupadi_satyabhama.summary: Krishna's wife Satyabhama asks Draupadi what charm keeps her five husbands devoted. Draupadi says charms and manipulation destroy trust, then describes her own exhaustive care of the household.

prasang:mbh.p.savitri.title: Savitri and Satyavan
prasang:mbh.p.savitri.lesson: Steady love and clear speech can face even death. Determination carries what fear would drop.
prasang:mbh.p.savitri.summary: Princess Savitri marries Satyavan knowing he will die within a year. On the fated day she follows Yama, the lord of death, speaking such wisdom about goodness and friendship that he grants boon after boon, until she wins back her husband's life.

prasang:mbh.p.nala_damayanti.title: Nala and Damayanti
prasang:mbh.p.nala_damayanti.lesson: Compulsions can take everything. Loyalty and patience can still bring you home.
prasang:mbh.p.nala_damayanti.summary: King Nala, possessed by the spirit Kali, gambles away his kingdom to his brother and abandons Damayanti in the forest. Years of separation and disguise follow, until Nala masters the dice and the two are reunited.

prasang:mbh.p.vyadha_gita.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang:mbh.p.vyadha_gita.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.
prasang:mbh.p.vyadha_gita.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.

prasang:mbh.p.yaksha_prashna.title: Yaksha Prashna: the questions at the lake
prasang:mbh.p.yaksha_prashna.lesson: Answer life's questions with a steady mind, and let kindness outweigh advantage.
prasang:mbh.p.yaksha_prashna.summary: One by one, four Pandavas drink from a lake against a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's riddles instead, and when offered one brother's life, chooses his stepmother's son Nakula, out of fairness.

prasang:mbh.p.yudhishthira_grief.title: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasang:mbh.p.yudhishthira_grief.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.
prasang:mbh.p.yudhishthira_grief.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.

prasang:mbh.p.ashma_gita.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang:mbh.p.ashma_gita.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.
prasang:mbh.p.ashma_gita.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.

prasang:mbh.p.sixteen_kings.title: The sixteen kings: Narada consoles Srinjaya
prasang:mbh.p.sixteen_kings.lesson: Everyone we love is mortal; you are not singled out. Grief can still be met with care.
prasang:mbh.p.sixteen_kings.summary: Krishna tells Yudhishthira how Narada consoled King Srinjaya, whose son had died, by recounting sixteen legendary kings far greater than his son who also died. Moved, Srinjaya listens, and Narada restores the boy.

prasang:mbh.p.friends_kin.title: Bhishma on friends and kinsmen
prasang:mbh.p.friends_kin.lesson: A true friend isn't stung by your success. Family is difficult, and still your refuge.
prasang:mbh.p.friends_kin.summary: Bhishma explains the kinds of friends, how to recognise the best friend, and the double nature of relatives: they can be rivals, yet when outsiders wrong you, family is your refuge.

prasang:mbh.p.krishna_narada_kin.title: Krishna's family troubles: the weapon not made of iron
prasang:mbh.p.krishna_narada_kin.lesson: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.
prasang:mbh.p.krishna_narada_kin.summary: Even Krishna struggles with his clan: he does their work, bears their harsh words, and feels like the mother of two gamblers playing each other. Narada tells him the only weapon that works is soft: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.

prasang:mbh.p.brihaspati_speech.title: Brihaspati on winning people with speech
prasang:mbh.p.brihaspati_speech.lesson: Kind words, spoken first and with warmth, win more than gifts.
prasang:mbh.p.brihaspati_speech.summary: Indra asks Brihaspati what single thing wins people over. Gentle, welcoming speech, says Brihaspati: speak first, with a smile; a gift without kind words pleases no one.

prasang:mbh.p.mother_father_teacher.title: Bhishma on mother, father and teacher
prasang:mbh.p.mother_father_teacher.lesson: Honour the people who raised and taught you; a mother's worth is beyond measure.
prasang:mbh.p.mother_father_teacher.summary: Asked which duty matters most, Bhishma names honouring one's mother, father and teachers, ranks the mother above all, and the teacher who gives knowledge highest of all.

prasang:mbh.p.kshemadarshi.title: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang:mbh.p.kshemadarshi.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.
prasang:mbh.p.kshemadarshi.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.

prasang:mbh.p.ganga_sagara.title: The river and the reeds
prasang:mbh.p.ganga_sagara.lesson: Bend with the flood and you stand again after it passes.
prasang:mbh.p.ganga_sagara.summary: The Ocean asks the rivers why they uproot great trees but never the reeds. Ganga answers: the reed bends when the flood comes and stands again after; the rigid tree breaks.

prasang:mbh.p.bearing_slander.title: Bhishma on bearing slander
prasang:mbh.p.bearing_slander.lesson: Careless critics show their own faults. Let their words pass like a crow's cawing.
prasang:mbh.p.bearing_slander.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to respond when a harsh fool abuses you in public. Bhishma: let it pass like a crow cawing; the slanderer only displays his own faults.

prasang:mbh.p.cat_mouse.title: The cat and the mouse
prasang:mbh.p.cat_mouse.lesson: Sometimes you must cooperate with a rival; do it with clear eyes.
prasang:mbh.p.cat_mouse.summary: Caught between a mongoose, an owl and a trapped cat, the mouse Palita makes a deal: he will gnaw the cat free if the cat protects him. Both keep the bargain, then part warily.

prasang:mbh.p.bharadvaja_counsel.title: Bharadvaja's counsel on gentleness and firmness
prasang:mbh.p.bharadvaja_counsel.summary: A king asks how to deal with rivals. Most of the answer is hard-edged statecraft, but one line holds: gentleness wins over both the gentle and the harsh.

prasang:mbh.p.pigeon_fowler.title: The pigeons and the fowler
prasang:mbh.p.pigeon_fowler.lesson: Kindness can shame cruelty. Wherever the one you love is, that is home.
prasang:mbh.p.pigeon_fowler.summary: A storm-soaked fowler shelters under a tree after trapping a female pigeon. Her mate, grieving, still honours the fowler as a guest, lights a fire for him and, having nothing else, offers himself as food. The shaken fowler gives up hunting.

prasang:mbh.p.gautama_ungrateful.title: Gautama the ungrateful
prasang:mbh.p.gautama_ungrateful.lesson: Gratitude is the root of every friendship. Betraying a benefactor poisons everything after.
prasang:mbh.p.gautama_ungrateful.summary: A destitute brahmin, Gautama, is fed and sheltered by a kind crane, Rajadharma, and made rich by the crane's friend. On the way home he kills his sleeping benefactor for food. Bhishma ends: there is atonement for many wrongs, none for ingratitude.

prasang:mbh.p.senajit_brahmin.title: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang:mbh.p.senajit_brahmin.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.
prasang:mbh.p.senajit_brahmin.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.

prasang:mbh.p.pingala.title: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
prasang:mbh.p.pingala.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.
prasang:mbh.p.pingala.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.

prasang:mbh.p.medhavin.title: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasang:mbh.p.medhavin.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.
prasang:mbh.p.medhavin.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.

prasang:mbh.p.shampaka.title: Shampaka on having little
prasang:mbh.p.shampaka.lesson: Holding tight breeds anxiety. Letting go is what lets you sleep.
prasang:mbh.p.shampaka.summary: A brahmin named Shampaka, in rags and poor, tells Bhishma why he weighed having nothing against a kingdom: the rich are always anxious, and without letting go no one sleeps without fear.

prasang:mbh.p.manki.title: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
prasang:mbh.p.manki.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.
prasang:mbh.p.manki.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.

prasang:mbh.p.bodhya.title: Bodhya's teachers
prasang:mbh.p.bodhya.lesson: Learn from everything. Drop what makes you a target, and give your work full attention.
prasang:mbh.p.bodhya.summary: Asked how he found peace, the sage Bodhya names his teachers: Pingala, the osprey that dropped its scrap of meat and was left alone, the snake, the deer, the arrow-maker so absorbed he did not see the king pass, and a girl's bangle.

prasang:mbh.p.ajagara.title: The python-sage (Ajagara vrata)
prasang:mbh.p.ajagara.lesson: Take what comes gladly; stop chasing what's out of reach.
prasang:mbh.p.ajagara.summary: Prahlada meets a sage who lives like a python, taking what comes and not chasing. The sage explains how ceasing to chase made him content.

prasang:mbh.p.kashyapa_jackal.title: Kashyapa and the jackal: the gift of hands
prasang:mbh.p.kashyapa_jackal.lesson: You already have what others long for. Craving is a fire that more fuel only feeds.
prasang:mbh.p.kashyapa_jackal.summary: A young brahmin, Kashyapa, knocked down by a rich man's chariot, wants to die in humiliation. A jackal tells him how lucky he is to have hands and a human life, and that craving grows like fire fed with wood. The jackal is Indra.

prasang:mbh.p.bali_indra.title: Bali and Indra: the fortune that moves on
prasang:mbh.p.bali_indra.lesson: Success is on loan. Don't gloat in a good season or despair in a bad one.
prasang:mbh.p.bali_indra.summary: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his defeated rival Bali living as a donkey in an empty house and mocks him. Bali calmly answers that fortune has lived with a thousand Indras before, that time gives and takes, and that this is a season for calm.

prasang:mbh.p.tuladhara_jajali.title: Tuladhara and Jajali: the merchant who taught the ascetic
prasang:mbh.p.tuladhara_jajali.lesson: Goodness is everyday fairness and friendliness, not spiritual display.
prasang:mbh.p.tuladhara_jajali.summary: The ascetic Jajali, proud because birds nest in his matted hair, is told to learn from a trader in Varanasi. Tuladhara teaches that right living is being a friend to all in thought, word and deed, and dealing fairly.

prasang:mbh.p.chirakari.title: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang:mbh.p.chirakari.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.
prasang:mbh.p.chirakari.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.

prasang:mbh.p.hamsa_gita.title: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang:mbh.p.hamsa_gita.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.
prasang:mbh.p.hamsa_gita.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.

prasang:mbh.p.narada_shuka.title: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang:mbh.p.narada_shuka.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.
prasang:mbh.p.narada_shuka.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.

prasang:mbh.p.daiva_purushakara.title: Fate or effort? Brahma's answer
prasang:mbh.p.daiva_purushakara.lesson: Luck is the seed, effort the field. Nothing grows without the field.
prasang:mbh.p.daiva_purushakara.summary: Yudhishthira asks which is stronger, destiny or human effort. Bhishma quotes Brahma: destiny is the seed, effort the field; without the field, the seed bears nothing.

prasang:mbh.p.karma_fruits.title: Bhishma on what ages and what doesn't
prasang:mbh.p.karma_fruits.lesson: Everything in us ages except wanting. Notice it.
prasang:mbh.p.karma_fruits.summary: Bhishma explains how deeds follow their doer, and observes that hair, teeth, eyes and ears grow old while craving alone stays young.

prasang:mbh.p.parrot_tree.title: The parrot who stayed with the withered tree
prasang:mbh.p.parrot_tree.lesson: Loyalty means staying through the bad season, not only the good.
prasang:mbh.p.parrot_tree.summary: A hunter's poisoned arrow withers the tree where a parrot has always lived. The parrot refuses to leave it. Indra, moved by its loyalty, restores the tree.

prasang:mbh.p.achara.title: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasang:mbh.p.achara.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.
prasang:mbh.p.achara.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.

prasang:mbh.p.brothers.title: Bhishma on elder and younger siblings
prasang:mbh.p.brothers.lesson: Overlook small faults, correct gently, share fairly, and don't let outsiders divide you.
prasang:mbh.p.brothers.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat the younger ones. Bhishma: overlook small faults and correct gently, beware outsiders who sow division, divide property equally, and honour the mother above all.

prasang:mbh.p.brihaspati_golden_rule.title: Brihaspati's golden rule
prasang:mbh.p.brihaspati_golden_rule.lesson: Don't do to others what would hurt you.
prasang:mbh.p.brihaspati_golden_rule.summary: Brihaspati sums up all of right conduct in one line: don't do to others what would hurt you.

prasang:mbh.p.inner_war.title: Krishna on the war within
prasang:mbh.p.inner_war.lesson: The hardest battle is with your own mind, and no one else can fight it for you.
prasang:mbh.p.inner_war.summary: As Yudhishthira still grieves, Krishna tells him his real battle has begun: one fought alone, with his own mind, where 'mine' is death and 'not mine' is freedom.

prasang:mbh.p.kama_gita.title: Kama Gita: the song of Desire
prasang:mbh.p.kama_gita.lesson: A craving fought only with force comes back in a new form. Redirect it instead.
prasang:mbh.p.kama_gita.summary: Krishna quotes Desire's own boast: whoever fights me with weapons, rituals, scripture, austerity or even the wish for liberation finds me reborn in that very method.

prasang:mbh.p.anugita_ambarisha.title: Ambarisha's song: the kingdom within
prasang:mbh.p.anugita_ambarisha.lesson: Master your own greed. That is the only kingdom worth ruling.
prasang:mbh.p.anugita_ambarisha.summary: King Ambarisha realises that the enemy he must conquer is his own greed, and sings that mastering it is the only kingdom worth having.

prasang:mbh.p.uttanka.title: Uttanka confronts Krishna
prasang:mbh.p.uttanka.lesson: You can try your best for peace and still fail. Others' choices are not your guilt.
prasang:mbh.p.uttanka.summary: Returning home after the war, Krishna meets the sage Uttanka, who is furious that Krishna let the cousins destroy each other and threatens to curse him. Krishna explains that he tried hard for peace and was refused, and calms him.

prasang:mbh.p.mongoose.title: The golden mongoose and the handful of flour
prasang:mbh.p.mongoose.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.
prasang:mbh.p.mongoose.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's lavish horse sacrifice, a half-golden mongoose declares it worth less than a poor family's gift. In a famine, a gleaner, his wife, son and daughter-in-law each gave their last handful of flour to a hungry guest; rolling in the spilt flour turned half the mongoose to gold.

prasang:vr.p.krauncha.title: Grief becomes the first verse
prasang:vr.p.krauncha.lesson: Grief can be turned into something that helps others; even a sage regrets words spoken in pain.
prasang:vr.p.krauncha.summary: Valmiki sees a hunter shoot one of a pair of mating cranes and hears the survivor cry. His grief bursts out as a curse that falls into rhythm; he regrets the words but realises they are a new kind of verse. Brahma tells him to use it to tell Ram's story.

prasang:vr.p.letting_ram_go.title: Dasharatha lets his son go
prasang:vr.p.letting_ram_go.lesson: Letting a child go out into the world can be the most loving thing a parent does.
prasang:vr.p.letting_ram_go.summary: The sage Vishvamitra asks the king for his teenage son Ram to protect a ritual. Dasharatha, who waited years for a child, refuses and offers himself and his army instead. His guru reminds him of his word and that the sage asks for Ram's own growth, and the king lets him go.

prasang:vr.p.bhagiratha.title: Bhagiratha brings the Ganga down
prasang:vr.p.bhagiratha.lesson: Some goals take longer than one effort or one lifetime; keep going and others' work is not wasted.
prasang:vr.p.bhagiratha.summary: King Sagara's sixty thousand sons are burnt to ash; only the Ganga's water can free them. Sagara, his grandson Anshuman and Anshuman's son Dilipa each try and die without success. Bhagiratha finally persists until the river descends, and Brahma honours him for finishing what three generations began.

prasang:vr.p.vasishtha_cow.title: The king who wanted the cow
prasang:vr.p.vasishtha_cow.lesson: Envy and force cannot take what someone will not give; real power is built inside.
prasang:vr.p.vasishtha_cow.summary: King Vishvamitra is feasted by the sage Vasishtha and covets the wish-granting cow that made it possible. Vasishtha refuses every offer; the king takes her by force and is routed, then fails again with divine weapons. Humbled, he resolves to transform himself through inner discipline instead of force.

prasang:vr.p.vishvamitra_menaka.title: Ten years gone: Vishvamitra and Menaka
prasang:vr.p.vishvamitra_menaka.lesson: Lost years are not the end; notice, stop blaming, and begin again.
prasang:vr.p.vishvamitra_menaka.summary: Deep into his effort to transform himself, Vishvamitra falls for the nymph Menaka and ten years pass like a day. When he wakes up to it, he is ashamed, lets her go kindly rather than blaming her, and starts again. Brahma tells him he is not there yet: he must first master his senses.

prasang:vr.p.vishvamitra_anger.title: Vishvamitra loses his temper, and begins again
prasang:vr.p.vishvamitra_anger.lesson: Relapses happen; a clear vow and steady practice can make anger lose its grip, and rivals can become friends.
prasang:vr.p.vishvamitra_anger.summary: Tested again, Vishvamitra explodes and curses the nymph Rambha, losing the fruit of his long effort. He vows not to give way to anger or speak in it, keeps a thousand-year silence, and this time obstacles shake him but anger cannot get in. He reaches his goal, and his old rival Vasishtha embraces him as a friend.

prasang:vr.p.ram_sita_marriage.title: Ram and Sita's early marriage
prasang:vr.p.ram_sita_marriage.lesson: Love deepens by paying attention to who the other person really is.
prasang:vr.p.ram_sita_marriage.summary: Back in Ayodhya after the wedding, Ram and Sita settle into married life. Valmiki notes that their love, though it began as an arranged match, deepened because each came to know and value the other; she could read his heart without words.

prasang:vr.p.ram_character.title: What Ram was like
prasang:vr.p.ram_character.lesson: Character shows in small habits: speaking first and gently, remembering kindness, forgetting slights.
prasang:vr.p.ram_character.summary: Before the crisis, Valmiki and the citizens describe the young prince: gentle in speech, unprovoked by harshness, pleased by one kindness and forgetful of a hundred wrongs, humble about his strength, attentive to ordinary people's lives.

prasang:vr.p.kaikeyi_boons.title: Kaikeyi's boons and the king's blind promise
prasang:vr.p.kaikeyi_boons.lesson: Envy grows when fed; never promise before you know what you are being asked.
prasang:vr.p.kaikeyi_boons.summary: The maid Manthara works on Queen Kaikeyi's insecurity until she is consumed by fear for her son's future. Kaikeyi makes the doting old king promise before she names her wish, then demands Ram's exile and Bharata's coronation. Bound by his word, Dasharatha pleads, rages and collapses.

prasang:vr.p.ram_accepts_exile.title: Ram accepts exile
prasang:vr.p.ram_accepts_exile.lesson: You cannot control the news; you can control the person who walks out of the room.
prasang:vr.p.ram_accepts_exile.summary: On the morning of his coronation, Ram is summoned and told by Kaikeyi that he must go into the forest for fourteen years. He agrees without anger, and is hurt only that his father could not tell him himself. He walks out showing no change of mind, already thinking of those he must comfort.

prasang:vr.p.kausalya_consents.title: Kausalya lets Ram go
prasang:vr.p.kausalya_consents.lesson: Love sometimes means staying behind to care for someone else.
prasang:vr.p.kausalya_consents.summary: Ram's mother faints at the news and begs to come with him. Ram gently refuses, asks her to look after his grieving father, and wins her blessing for the journey.

prasang:vr.p.lakshman_anger_exile.title: Lakshman's fury, Ram's calm
prasang:vr.p.lakshman_anger_exile.lesson: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.
prasang:vr.p.lakshman_anger_exile.summary: Lakshman is enraged by the injustice and wants to seize the throne by force. Ram calms him: set aside the insult, don't torment yourself, the setback may lead somewhere better. Lakshman answers that effort, not fate, decides; both views are given their due.

prasang:vr.p.sita_chooses.title: Sita chooses to go
prasang:vr.p.sita_chooses.lesson: A partnership means making big decisions together, and listening when the other has decided.
prasang:vr.p.sita_chooses.summary: Ram asks Sita to stay safely in Ayodhya. She refuses, argues, laughs at his fears and insists: the hardships he lists are nothing if they face them together. Ram listens, realises he had not understood how determined she was, and agrees.

prasang:vr.p.father_one_more_night.title: One more night: Ram leaves his father
prasang:vr.p.father_one_more_night.lesson: Goodbyes to ageing parents are hard; leave with love and a promise to return.
prasang:vr.p.father_one_more_night.summary: The broken king begs Ram to stay one more night so his parents can see him. Ram gently refuses, saying a promise made must be kept and he will return in fourteen years. Dasharatha embraces him and collapses.

prasang:vr.p.sumitra_sends_lakshman.title: Sumitra sends Lakshman with Ram
prasang:vr.p.sumitra_sends_lakshman.lesson: Home is the people you are with; you can carry it into any wilderness.
prasang:vr.p.sumitra_sends_lakshman.summary: As the exiles leave, Lakshman's mother blesses him: treat Ram as your father, Sita as your mother, and the forest as home. She tells him to go happily.

prasang:vr.p.sumitra_consoles.title: Sumitra sits with Kausalya
prasang:vr.p.sumitra_consoles.lesson: When a child leaves, a friend who shares the ache helps more than advice.
prasang:vr.p.sumitra_consoles.summary: Kausalya weeps for her son gone to the forest. Her co-queen Sumitra, whose own son has gone too, comforts her: he went for a good reason, he is not alone, and you will see him again.

prasang:vr.p.leaving_sleeping_city.title: Ram slips away from the loyal crowd
prasang:vr.p.leaving_sleeping_city.lesson: Leaders protect people from their troubles; they don't pull others into their own.
prasang:vr.p.leaving_sleeping_city.summary: Thousands of citizens follow Ram into the wilderness, determined to bring him back. At dawn he slips away while they sleep so they will go home rather than suffer for his sake.

prasang:vr.p.ram_message_home.title: Ram's messages home
prasang:vr.p.ram_message_home.lesson: Even when a parent fails you, you can choose to protect their dignity.
prasang:vr.p.ram_message_home.summary: The charioteer returns and delivers Ram's messages: honour our father in his old age, be kind to all three mothers including Kaikeyi. He also delivers Lakshman's furious words about their father, showing two very different ways sons respond to a parent's failure.

prasang:vr.p.kausalya_dasharatha.title: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang:vr.p.kausalya_dasharatha.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.
prasang:vr.p.kausalya_dasharatha.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.

prasang:vr.p.shravana.title: The boy at the river: Dasharatha's old guilt
prasang:vr.p.shravana.lesson: Carelessness can wound for decades; owning it honestly is the only way to carry it.
prasang:vr.p.shravana.summary: Dying of grief, Dasharatha confesses to Kausalya that as a young prince he shot at a sound in the dark and killed a boy filling water for his blind, aged parents. He took the water to them and told them the truth himself. The father cursed him to lose a son as they had, and now, longing for Ram, the king dies at midnight.

prasang:vr.p.bharata_returns.title: Bharata comes home too late
prasang:vr.p.bharata_returns.lesson: Missing a parent's death far from home is its own grief; let yourself feel it.
prasang:vr.p.bharata_returns.summary: Bharata, living at his uncle's court, has a nightmare and is summoned home. He finds the city silent and learns from his mother that his father has died while he was away, and then that Ram is in exile because of her.

prasang:vr.p.bharata_blamed.title: Bharata wrongly blamed
prasang:vr.p.bharata_blamed.lesson: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.
prasang:vr.p.bharata_blamed.summary: Bharata turns on his mother in fury. Then Ram's grieving mother assumes he plotted it all, and her words cut him like a needle in a wound. He falls at her feet and swears his innocence until she believes him.

prasang:vr.p.funeral_and_manthara.title: At the pyre, and the hand that stopped
prasang:vr.p.funeral_and_manthara.lesson: Grief and rage come together; one calm person can stop a moment we'd regret forever.
prasang:vr.p.funeral_and_manthara.summary: The brothers perform their father's rites and collapse in grief; the family priest lifts them up. When Shatrughna drags Manthara before him in rage, Bharata stops him: Ram would never forgive cruelty done in his name.

prasang:vr.p.bharata_refuses.title: Bharata refuses the throne
prasang:vr.p.bharata_refuses.lesson: Not every gain is worth taking; integrity sometimes means refusing what you are handed.
prasang:vr.p.bharata_refuses.summary: The court offers Bharata the kingdom his mother won for him. He refuses before the whole assembly, says it belongs to his brother, and sets out with the army and the city to bring Ram back.

prasang:vr.p.guha_suspects.title: Guha's suspicion and Bharata's grief
prasang:vr.p.guha_suspects.lesson: Prepare if you must, but find out someone's intent before you judge them.
prasang:vr.p.guha_suspects.summary: Ram's friend Guha sees Bharata's army and assumes he has come to kill Ram. He prepares to block the river but goes to meet him first. Learning Bharata's intent, he becomes his guide and shows him the grass bed where Ram slept, where Bharata vows to live as an ascetic until Ram returns.

prasang:vr.p.lakshman_suspects_bharata.title: Lakshman suspects Bharata
prasang:vr.p.lakshman_suspects_bharata.lesson: Don't assume the worst of family on the strength of what you see from a distance.
prasang:vr.p.lakshman_suspects_bharata.summary: From a tree at Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharata's army and is sure he has come to finish them. Ram stops him: Bharata has never wronged us; why suspect him now? And no kingdom is worth winning through wrong.

prasang:vr.p.statecraft_questions.title: Ram's questions to Bharata
prasang:vr.p.statecraft_questions.lesson: Good leaders consult wisely, act promptly, and listen to people with no power.
prasang:vr.p.statecraft_questions.summary: Meeting Bharata at Chitrakoot, Ram asks a long series of questions about how he is running the kingdom: whom he consults, how quickly he acts, whether he listens to the falsely accused.

prasang:vr.p.chitrakoot_reunion.title: The brothers meet at Chitrakoot
prasang:vr.p.chitrakoot_reunion.lesson: A rift can close in one embrace; grief shared between siblings is lighter.
prasang:vr.p.chitrakoot_reunion.summary: Bharata finds Ram in bark clothes and falls weeping at his feet, blaming himself. Ram embraces him, tells him he sees no fault in him, and asks him not to blame his mother. Then Ram learns their father is dead and grieves that he was not there.

prasang:vr.p.impermanence_teaching.title: Ram on why grief must not rule us
prasang:vr.p.impermanence_teaching.lesson: Everything that comes together parts; let that make you gentler, not hopeless.
prasang:vr.p.impermanence_teaching.summary: Bharata begs Ram to return and rule. Ram answers with a teaching on impermanence: everything gathered runs out, everything rising falls, people meet like logs on the ocean and drift apart. Grieve, but do not let grief overturn your duty.

prasang:vr.p.jabali.title: Jabali's doubt
prasang:vr.p.jabali.lesson: Doubt deserves a hearing; answer it with how you choose to live.
prasang:vr.p.jabali.summary: The priest Jabali argues that nobody belongs to anyone, rituals are empty and only the present matters, so Ram should take the throne. Ram answers that conduct, not claims, shows who we are, and that people follow the example of those who lead.

prasang:vr.p.sandals.title: The sandals: a compromise between brothers
prasang:vr.p.sandals.lesson: When neither can give way, find a form that honours both; and let go of blame.
prasang:vr.p.sandals.summary: Bharata threatens to fast at Ram's door until he returns. Ram persuades him to rise, and they reach a compromise: Bharata takes Ram's sandals to rule in his name. At parting Ram asks him to drop his resentment of their mother.

prasang:vr.p.nandigram.title: Bharata's fourteen years at Nandigram
prasang:vr.p.nandigram.lesson: Waiting can be active: keep faith by taking care of what was entrusted to you.
prasang:vr.p.nandigram.summary: Bharata refuses to live in the palace. From a village hut he governs in the name of Ram's sandals, dressed as an ascetic, holding everything in trust and waiting fourteen years for his brother.

prasang:vr.p.sita_nonviolence.title: Sita questions the weapon
prasang:vr.p.sita_nonviolence.lesson: Disagree with someone you love openly; advice is a sign of care.
prasang:vr.p.sita_nonviolence.summary: Sita worries that Ram, carrying weapons among peaceful hermits, will be drawn into needless violence.
